Meanwhile, the company was criticized after it was revealed that SGI had not acquired the Information Security Management System (ISMS) or the Personal Information & Information Security Management System (ISMS-P) certifications. These certifications assess whether an organization has established appropriate safeguards for information and data privacy. They are, even for financial companies, not required by law in Korea.

A hacker operating under the pseudonym ByteToBreach allegedly breached Seychelles Commercial Bank (SCB) on 5 February 2025 and subsequently exfiltrated over 2 GB of customer data from its online banking systems, beginning on 4 July. The attacker claimed to have exploited a vulnerability in Oracle WebLogic Server to gain access, and later exfiltrated the data. According to cybersecurity firm Resecurity, the leaked dataset includes names, phone numbers, email addresses, account types and balances - some associated with government-labelled accounts. The attacker also claimed to have decrypted portions of the data using keys obtained from SCB’s internal environment, specifically within its Oracle Flexcube Private Banking (FCDB) platform. SCB confirmed the breach on 12 July, stating that personal information of internet banking customers was exposed but no funds were accessed. Internet banking services were temporarily suspended, and the bank urged customers to use ATMs or visit branches. Law enforcement and the Central Bank of Seychelles were notified. ByteToBreach attempted to extort the bank and, after receiving no response, began contacting customers directly and selling the stolen data on dark web forums.

The website of the Hanover S-Bahn was rendered inaccessible for several hours following a suspected DDoS attack on 24 July 2025 - the second such disruption this month. According to a spokesperson, the site became unavailable in the early afternoon when malicious traffic overloaded the servers, preventing normal access and functionality. The attack, believed to be similar to one that occurred on 9 July, involved flooding the website with excessive external requests, causing the system to crash with a ‘Bad Gateway’ error. IT teams from Hanover S-Bahn and its parent company, Transdev Group, responded by activating network filters to restore service within a few hours.

Unknown hackers targeted Stolichki, a major Moscow-based pharmacy chain, disrupting its accounting and sales systems, on 29 July 2025. The incident forced the temporary closure of nearly 900 outlets across the capital. Stolichki’s administration convened a crisis management team to coordinate the response, while technical staff worked to restore affected systems and resume operations.

The official website of the city of Erfurt (Erfurt.de) was temporarily knocked offline following a targeted DDoS attack on 29 July 2025. The incident began around 8:30 am and overwhelmed the site with up to 4.5 million requests per hour, rendering it inaccessible for several hours. The city’s IT department responded swiftly and implemented mitigation measures. By approximately 1 pm, access to the site had been restored.

Ukrainian military intelligence (GUR) conducted a major cyber operation against the servers of the Russian-installed administration in occupied Crimea, extracting approximately 100 terabytes of data in around 25 July 2025. Material obtained during the breach was subsequently transferred to law enforcement for further analysis, including thousands of classified documents and detailed records on Ukrainian children who had been abducted from the occupied territories of Kherson, Zaporizhzhia, Donetsk and Luhansk. The secured documents contained identifying information and personal details of deported children, many of whom had been left without guardianship. Some were reportedly placed for adoption by Russian citizens in violation of international law. According to GUR spokesman Andrii Yusov, the obtained data is critical for documenting Russia’s war crimes and will support ongoing efforts to locate and return the abducted children to Ukraine.

Silent Crow, a pro-Ukrainian hacker group, breached Rostelecom in January 2025, after accessing the IT systems of one of its contractors, and leaked customer information, although Rostelecom claimed that no sensitive data was stolen. The group claimed responsibility for the breach.

Title (Company): Unified Medical Information and Analytical System (EMIAS)
Description: Prior to 20 July 2025, Silent Crow, a pro-Ukrainian hacker group, breached Moscow's Unified Medical Information and Analytical System, also known as the EMIAS medical system. The attackers gained full access to the system, claiming administrative control, and exfiltrated 17 TB of sensitive data, including patient records, diagnostics, prescriptions, and internal access coordinates of staff. The hackers then disabled access to the system and deleted the backup data storage. The attack was reported by Silent Crow on 20 July 2025 on Telegram, and later disclosed to the public through articles published on 29 July 2025.

On 25 July 2025, the French telecommunications provider Orange sustained a compromise of one of its information systems, resulting in disruptions to services for some business customers and public services mainly in France. The company's security teams, including experts from its subsidiary Orange Cyberdefense, were immediately alerted and worked to isolate potentially affected services and limit impacts. The incident lasted only a few hours. The next day, essential services were restored. However, some management platforms for business customers in France remained temporarily inaccessible. A complaint was filed for infringing the company's information system, and an investigation was launched with the support of relevant authorities. The affected services were expected to return by the morning of 30 July 2025.

Title (Company): Russia's National Cyber Incident Response Team (CERT)
Description: The hacktivist collective Cyberpartisans and pro-Ukrainian Silent Crow compromised Russia's National Cyber Incident Response Team (CERT) in March 2025. The attackers claimed to have struck at the heart of the regime's cyber defence, declaring that CERT was an open gateway. The incident was reported by Ukrainian media on 29 July 2025.

On 28 July 2025, Acea, a Roman multi-utility company that manages water, energy, and environmental services, was targeted by a ransomware attack claimed by the collective World Leaks. World Leaks, which emerged in early 2025 as a branding of the Ransomware-as-a-Service Hunters International group, focuses exclusively on information theft and extortion. The extent of the damage and the amount of sensitive data extracted from Acea's business databases were not yet clear at the time of reporting, with technical checks and investigations still underway. RansomNews disclosed the attack, and World Leaks published exfiltrated data on X, with a declared expiry date of 29 July 2025.

In March 2025, the Belarusian national CERT, responsible for protecting the country's infrastructure, was compromised by pro-Ukrainian Silent Crow and Cyberpartisans. The hacktivists breached the CERT's most protected server, exfiltrating data including internal databases, site source codes with configurations, and gaining access to email and internal services. Silent Crow and Cyberpartisans claimed responsibility for the breach.

On 10 July 2025, Ukrainian CERT (CERT-UA) discovered a breach involving the LameHug malware. The attackers used an AI-powered large language model to generate commands that were executed on compromised Windows systems, gathering system information and searching for Office, PDF, and TXT files in common folders. The stolen data was stored locally before being exfiltrated via SFTP or HTTP POST. CERT-UA attributed the attack with medium confidence to the Russian state-sponsored group APT28 and informed the public about the attack on 17 July 2025.

Title (Company): McKenzie Memorial Hospital - McKenzie Health System
Description: McKenzie Health System, a healthcare provider in Sandusky, Michigan, experienced a network intrusion between 14 and 15 April 2025, during which an unauthorized party gained access to internal systems and potentially compromised files containing personal information. The breach, internally discovered on 15 April and investigated through June, affected 54,016 individuals. The exposed data may include full names, Social Security numbers, and financial account details. McKenzie concluded its investigation on 19 June and began mailing notification letters on 24 July 2025. This marks McKenzie Health System’s second data breach in three years.

Unknown threat actors launched a ransomware attack against Infinite Services, a New York-based provider of physical therapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy, and counselling services, on 5 May 2025. The attack was first detected when employees were unable to access the network due to suspicious activity. The attackers compromised a server containing personally identifiable information of patients and employees, including names, addresses, Social Security numbers, member identification numbers, dates of birth, and health insurance details. External counsel SpencerFane notified the New Hampshire Attorney General, and the full scope of the breach was determined by 23 June 2025. Although there was communication with the attackers, no ransom was paid and no data has been published.

Unknown threat actors compromised the systems of Toppan Next Tech (TNT), a police printing vendor in Singapore, in a ransomware attack that occurred months before 18 July 2025. As a result, approximately 1,300 names and addresses of traffic offenders were published online. TNT had received the data from the Traffic Police, including names, addresses, NRIC numbers, and traffic violation details. However, only names and addresses were confirmed to have been leaked. The incident did not involve a breach of the Traffic Police’s systems. Authorities have found no indication that other sensitive data was circulated. The Cyber Security Agency of Singapore (CSA) and the police informed the public about the breach on 24 July 2025.

On 23 June 2023, the Akira Ransom Software group, a cyber crime syndicate, infiltrated KNP Logistics, a 158-year-old British shipping company, by predicting an employee's password, gaining unauthorized access to the company's system. The attackers then encrypted the data and locked the internal systems, demanding a ransom of approximately $5 million. The company, unable to pay the ransom, suffered total loss of data, ultimately leading to bankruptcy and 700 job losses. The incident was reported by the BBC, with KNP Logistics' director, Paul Abbott, linking the breach to a weak password. The Akira Ransom Software group claimed responsibility for the incident.

Title (Company): Not available - Not available - Not available - Not available - Unspecified universities - National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA)  - Not available - Not available - Asian telecommunications company - Not available - Not available - Energy companies - Not available - Not available - U.S. federal agencies - National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA) - Not available - U.S. Department of Homeland Security - U.S. state agencies
Description: At least three China-nexus threat actors (Linen Typhoon/APT27, Violet Typhoon/APT31 and Storm-2603) exploited two zero-day vulnerabilities (CVE-2025-53770 and CVE-2025-537701) in Microsoft's collaboration software SharePoint to breach multiple organizations globally including U.S. state and federal agencies, universities, energy companies, and an Asian telecommunications company.  The breaches affected tens of thousands of servers worldwide that host SharePoint locally, including those of organizations in the United States, Canada, Austria, Jordan, Mexico, Germany, Switzerland, Netherlands, South Africa, Australia, Spain, Brazil, and Asia. On 19 July 2025, Microsoft issued a customer guidance for the SharePoint vulnerabilities, recommending users to modify server settings or disconnect them from the internet. As of 22 July, Microsoft had released a patch for all supported versions of the software.  Abuse of the two zero days was first detected by the Dutch cybersecurity company Eye Security on 18 July. The observed intrusions leveraged the zero-day vulnerabilities along an exploit chain demonstrated earlier in May 2025 that takes advantage of two related SharePoint vulnerabilities (CVE-2025-49706 and CVE-2025-49704). The compromise allowed intruders to obtain cryptographic keys for breached servers. With this access, the threat actors are able to impersonate users and maintain persistence on compromised systems through backdoors even after security updates are installed to mitigate the vulnerabilities. In at least one instance reported by the Washington Post on 20 July, an official of an eastern US state noted losing access to a repository of documents informing the public about government services. Whether the data was deleted remained unclear at the time of reporting. On 21 July, the Washington Post further cited an assessment by Google’s Mandiant Consulting that deemed at least one China-nexus actor was involved in the early exploitation of the software flaws.  On 22 July, Microsoft Threat Intelligence reported that at least three China-linked threat actors—Linen Typhoon (APT27), Violet Typhoon (APT31), and Storm-2603—had exploited a SharePoint vulnerability for data theft and espionage. The United States, Canada, and Australia launched an investigation into the incident.

Title (Company): City of St. Paul - City of St. Paul - Digital Services - City of St. Paul - Libraries - City of St. Paul - Recreation Centers
Description: Critical systems in St. Paul, Minnesota, were targeted in a cyberattack that disrupted offline payments and digital services across libraries, recreation centres, and other city operations. The breach, first detected on 25 July through suspicious activity flagged by the city’s endpoint detection and response system, persisted through the weekend and significantly impaired essential services. In response, Governor Tim Walz issued an executive order activating the Minnesota National Guard to support mitigation efforts. Mayor Melvin Carter declared a state of local emergency on 29 July, authorizing the Emergency Management Department and Office of Technology and Communications to coordinate with state and federal partners. To contain the breach, the city initiated a complete network shutdown, disabling public internet terminals and Wi-Fi systems across municipal facilities. Libraries and recreation centres remained open but without internet access. The FBI and federal cybersecurity experts are leading the criminal investigation. On 10 August 2025, a city spokesperson confirmed to local news outlets the city was hit with a ransomware attack but said it has not paid the ransom. One day later, Interlock ransomware group claimed responsibility for the incident.

The Swiss-based private hospital operator Ameos Group detected a breach of its IT infrastructure on 7 July 2025, prompting a precautionary shutdown of digital systems across at the roughly 40 facilities the healthcare provider operates in Germany. The IT outage caused major disruptions: email communication failed, digital patient records became inaccessible, and services reverted to manual processes. Some emergency rooms and labs reported delays and rerouted patient transports, though patient care reportedly remained safe throughout. Ameos publicly stated that patient, employee, partner, and corporate contact data was stolen in the incident. The incident has triggered a criminal investigation by the State Criminal Police Office of Saxony-Anhalt in Germany, following a formal criminal complaint filed by Ameos. The hospital operator covers over 100 locations treating more than 500,000 patients annually.

Title (Company): Allianz Life Insurance Company of North America
Description: On 16 July 2025, Allianz Life Insurance Company of North America (Allianz Life) was breached by a threat actor using a social engineering technique to access a third-party cloud-based customer relationship management (CRM) system. The incident resulted in the exposure of personally identifiable data relating to the majority of Allianz Life’s 1.4 million customers, financial professionals and select employees. Allianz Life stated that the attack did not compromise its internal network or policy administration system. The company reported the incident to the FBI and initiated customer notifications. The breach only affected Allianz Life and not its parent company, Allianz SE. Public disclosure followed on 26 July 2025, via filings with the Maine Attorney General’s Office and subsequent media reporting. While Allianz Life has not confirmed the identity of the attacker, BleepingComputer noted that the breach may be linked to the ShinyHunters extortion group, which is thought to have significant overlap with the Scattered Spider group.

On 25 July 2025, Cathay Pacific Airways disclosed that approximately 1,000 membership accounts were accessed by unauthorized parties, primarily affecting members based in Hong Kong. The attackers used valid credentials previously exposed online and exploited a weakness in the secondary verification process to gain access. The breach allowed threat actors to view personal details and travel information and steal Asia Miles, although no credit card data was compromised. Cathay Pacific rectified the verification flaw, reinforced authentication measures, and worked to restore affected accounts and reinstate stolen Asia Miles. Most impacted members were contacted directly. The airline reported the incident to relevant authorities, including the Office of the Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data, and appointed an external expert to conduct an independent investigation.

Title (Company): Barbados Public Workers Cooperative Credit Union Limited (BPWCCUL)
Description: A sustained BIN attack was carried out by unknown cybercriminals against the Barbados Public Workers Cooperative Credit Union Limited (BPWCCUL), resulting in a loss of $1.29 million from the surplus that the credit union would have recorded over the past year. The incident occurred during the financial year which ended on 31 March 2025.  It was first reported by president Mark Hope in the credit union's annual report, published on 22 July 2025, disclosing that the threat actors compromised some members' Mastercard debit cards. The cybercriminals engaged in a systematic attempt to guess valid credit card details like the Bank Identification Number, expiration date, and card verification value (CVV), to carry out fraudulent acts, including purchases.

Unknown threat actors compromised the Kairos application used by France Travail, resulting in the unauthorized access of personal data belonging to approximately 340,000 jobseekers. The breach was traced to an account belonging to a training organization based in Isère, which had been infected with an infostealer designed to capture authentication credentials. The exposed data included names, dates of birth, France Travail identifiers, email and postal addresses, and phone numbers; passwords and financial information were not affected. The incident occurred on 12 July 2025 and was publicly disclosed by France Travail on 23 July 2025. In response, the organization closed the affected service, lodged a complaint with judicial authorities, and notified the CNIL. The Paris Public Prosecutor’s Office assigned the investigation to the BL2C (Brigade de lutte contre la cybercriminalité) for breach of an automated data processing system.

Universidad Mayor in Santiago, one of Chile’s largest private universities, was targeted by the DireWolf ransomware group in a cyberattack disclosed on 23 July 2025. The attack encrypted institutional servers and potentially exposed personal data. Despite the incident, academic activity remained unaffected and most services have since been restored.  DireWolf claimed responsibility for the attack. No data leaks had been confirmed at the time of reporting.

Unknown threat actors breached the internal IT systems of Colabor Group Inc., a Canadian food distributor, on 20 July 2025. The company immediately implemented containment measures, engaged external cybersecurity experts, and launched an investigation to determine the scope and impact of the incident. It remains unclear whether any customer, supplier, or employee data was compromised. In its disclosure statement from 21 July, company leadership expected the incident to cause temporary service disruptions until affected systems are fully restored.

Title (Company): Attorney General's Office of the State of San Luis Potosi (FGESLP)
Description: On 25 July 2025, a hacker known as 'Kazu' breached the online portal of the Attorney General’s Office of the State of San Luis Potosí (FGESLP) in Mexico, exploiting a structural vulnerability to obtain over 73,000 criminal history records bearing authentic digital stamps. The exposed database, totalling 36.4 GB and comprising 73,156 PDF files, included sensitive personal data and legal documentation. Kazu demanded $6,000 to withhold the leak and offered the full dataset for sale at $600 via a clandestine forum. Cybersecurity analyst Nicolas Azuara confirmed the presence of a critical flaw in the FGESLP website that enabled unauthorized access to criminal records by modifying URL parameters with valid credentials. The vulnerability, which may have been open to exploitation through leaked access data or infostealer-type malware, allowed attackers to exfiltrate confidential documents without authentication barriers.

Unknown threat actors breached the Fort Smith Public School District in Arkansas on or before 21 July 2025, disrupting phone and internet systems across the district. The incident was publicly disclosed by district communications specialist Addie Reith via a Facebook post on 21 July and in a statement to Talk Business & Politics on 23 July. The district engaged a third-party cybersecurity firm to assist with remediation efforts. While the attackers' identities and methods remain undisclosed, the breach was reported to all required agencies in line with Arkansas Department of Education guidelines. As of 24 July, system restoration was still in progress, though officials stated that the disruption was not expected to delay the school year, scheduled to begin on 13 August 2025.

Title (Company): US Department of Energy (DoE) - Unspecified Organisations - U.S. Department of Homeland Security - US Department of Education - California Independent System Operator - US Department of Health and Human Services - National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA)
Description: Chinese state-sponsored threat actors exploited zero-day vulnerabilities in Microsoft SharePoint Server, compromising over 400 organisations worldwide, including several US federal agencies and the National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA), according to Microsoft and cybersecurity researchers.  Microsoft confirmed that three threat groups - Linen Typhoon, Violet Typhoon (both state-sponsored) and Storm-2603 (a China-based actor) - exploited a vulnerability chain dubbed "ToolShell" targeting on-premises SharePoint servers exposed to the internet. The vulnerabilities (CVE-2025-53770 and CVE-2025-53771) allow authentication bypass and remote code execution. Initial exploitation began as early as 7 July 2025. The Dutch cybersecurity firm Eye Security first detected unusual activity on 18 July 2025 and subsequently identified dozens of compromised systems after scanning over 8,000 SharePoint instances. Affected sectors include government, defence, energy, healthcare and critical infrastructure. Confirmed victims include the US Departments of Energy, Homeland Security, Health and Human Services and Education, as well as the California Independent System Operator. A Department of Energy spokesperson stated that only a limited number of systems were affected and there was no evidence of classified data being compromised. Microsoft observed Storm-2603 deploying Warlock ransomware on compromised networks beginning 18 July 2025, disabling Microsoft Defender, modifying policy settings and attempting to exfiltrate cryptographic keys from SharePoint servers to maintain persistent access. CISA added the exploited CVEs to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue and instructed federal agencies to apply patches and conduct compromise assessments.

MuddyWater, a threat actor believed to be affiliated with the Iranian Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS), used a newly-discovered strain of the Android surveillance tool DCHSpy to primarily target regime adversaries, between June and July 2025. MuddyWater distributed the malware using spoofed URLs in Telegram and other messaging app channels, intended to draw targets to websites hosting malicious VPN and banking apps. The malware exfiltrated data from WhatsApp, files stored on devices, contacts, text messages, location and call logs, and was able to use device cameras and microphones to take photos and record audio. The threat actors relied on political lures, including websites containing links to malicious apps, with one lure involving Starlink, which provided Iranians with web access after the country's government imposed an internet blackout following Israel's attacks. Researchers from the cybersecurity firm Lookout detected the latest version of DCHSpy one week after Israel began its air campaign targeting Iran's nuclear program in June 2025, according to a company report published on 21 July 2025.

An unauthorised party breached Premier Health Partners (PHP) in Ohio between 7 June and 12 July 2023, potentially exposing sensitive information of certain individuals. The incident was discovered on 12 July 2023, prompting an internal investigation to determine its nature and scope. The investigation confirmed that files on specific Premier Health systems had been accessed and acquired during the breach period. Although there is no evidence suggesting the compromised data has been misused, the incident was reported to the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) on 12 October 2023 and is believed to have affected approximately 10,833 patients. Compromised data may have included patients'  name, date of birth, Social Security number, driver's license number or state issued identification number, passport number, individual taxpayer identification number, digital signature, login credentials, financial account information, medical information, and health insurance information. Premier Health Partners issued a press release and published a substitute notice on its website on 20 July 2025, disclosing the breach to the public after two years.

Unidentified threat actors breached the systems of Radiology Associates of Richmond between 2 and 6 April 2024, exposing the personal and health information of more than 1.4 million individuals. The incident was discovered internally and confirmed on 2 May 2025 following an investigation. External cybersecurity experts were engaged to secure the network, and affected individuals were notified beginning 1 July 2025, with credit monitoring offered to those whose Social Security numbers were compromised. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) reported that 1,419,091 people were impacted.

Anne Arundel Dermatology, a physician-owned dermatology group, was breached by an unauthorized party between 14 February and 13 May 2025, affecting approximately 1.9 million individuals. The breach, which involved access to files containing personal and health information, was detected and secured by the organization. An investigation launched on 20 May confirmed that sensitive data had been compromised, prompting precautionary notifications to affected individuals. The US Department of Health and Human Services reported the incident, which was publicly disclosed through a data breach notice. Anne Arundel Dermatology offered 24 months of identity protection services and advised individuals to monitor their account statements and credit reports.

On 19 July 2025, hackers breached CoinDCX, India’s leading cryptocurrency exchange, stealing approximately $44 million from one of the company’s internal operational accounts. The attackers exploited a sophisticated server breach, with initial activity traced to a wallet funded via Tornado Cash, a privacy-focused crypto mixer. A portion of the stolen assets was later bridged from Solana (SOL) to Ethereum (ETH). CoinDCX cofounders Neeraj Khandelwal and CEO Sumit Gupta disclosed the incident via X posts on the same day, assuring customers that their funds were unaffected as they are held in segregated wallets.  The company’s internal security and operations teams launched an investigation in collaboration with external cybersecurity partners to identify vulnerabilities, track the stolen funds, and bolster defences. CoinDCX temporarily suspended trading in the Web3 section as a precaution and announced plans to introduce a bug bounty programme to aid in the recovery effort. During July 2025, the IT security company Cyvers issued a report linking the attack to North Korean state-sponsored group Lazarus.

A Chinese state-sponsored hacking group, identified as UNC3886, compromised critical infrastructure in Singapore around 18 July 2025. The attackers targeted high-value sectors including defence, telecommunications, and technology, deploying custom backdoors on Juniper Networks routers, Fortinet devices, and VMware infrastructure to infiltrate sensitive systems. Singapore’s Coordinating Minister for National Security, K. Shanmugam, publicly acknowledged the incident in a speech on 18 July 2025.

Unknown hackers breached the Córdoba Police’s administrative systems, compromising labour records of police personnel. The intrusion was detected on 17 July 2025, prompting immediate containment measures. Authorities confirmed that no sensitive data was accessed and that public safety was not at risk.  A judicial investigation was initiated, with specialized teams conducting forensic analysis to determine the origin and method of the compromise.

A hacker suspected of ties to the Iranian government compromised the Arizona Secretary of State’s Office candidate portal, between 23 and 30 June 2025. The attacker uploaded malicious scripts to the server, replacing historical candidate images (2016–2024) with a photograph of former Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Musavi Khomeini. Some of the altered images linked to social media accounts, including a Telegram channel containing messages critical of US President Trump’s policies towards Iran. The intrusion occurred two days after a US bombing operation in Iran and was discovered by a staff member. The Arizona Secretary of State, Adrian Fontes, publicly disclosed the attack, noting that the hacker continued to target the Secretary of State’s website for nearly a week. Other Arizona state agencies were also reportedly targeted by the same IP addresses. Authorities confirmed that the intrusion did not affect election tabulation or results. The FBI, state Department of Homeland Security, and National Guard were engaged to support the investigation and response.

The Pro-Ukrainian hacktivist group BO Team (aka Black Owl) claimed to have breached Gaskar Group, a Russian drone factory. According to their telegram post, BO Team carried out the operation in collaboration with the Ukrainian Cyber Alliance and Ukraine’s military intelligence, destroying more than 250 systems, including 46 virtual servers and more than 200 workstations. In addition, the hackers wiped 47 terabytes of company data and 10 terabytes of backups. The data theft also included personal data of Gaskar Group employees. The incident was first reported on 15 July 2025.

On 25 November 2024, and 14 February 2025, Russian hackers, as part of the NoName057(16) campaign, carried out a DDoS attack on the taz newspaper website using a botnet, which affected the website's availability. The incident was reported by taz following their reporting on the police action against NoName057(16) in mid July 2025. From 14 to 17 July 2025, an international law enforcement operation code-named Eastwood was launched against NoName057(16). Coordinated by Europol and Eurojust, the operation involved simultaneous actions by authorities in Czechia, France, Finland, Germany, Italy, Lithuania, Poland, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, the Netherlands, and the United States, targeting individuals and digital infrastructure linked to the pro-Russian network. Operation Eastwood allowed for the deactivation of several hundred servers supporting the group’s DDoS activities. Overall, national authorities issued seven arrest warrants, including against six Russian nationals, over the suspected involvement in NoName057(16). The investigation further facilitated the arrest of two individuals in France and Spain. Law enforcement personally notified over 1,000 supporters of the group, including 15 suspected administrators, of their legal liability related to the participation in NoName057(16)‘s criminal activities.

Cookeville Regional Medical Center (CRMC), a 269-bed hospital in Tennessee, was targeted by a ransomware attack that started on 13 July 2025, causing an IT outage that slowed some scheduling and technology, but did not affect patient care. The hospital's information services security team worked with outside IT experts to investigate the incident, which was disclosed to the public through a Facebook post on 15 July 2025. On 2 August 2025, the ransomware group Rhysidia added CRMC to its leak site, claiming to have obtained medical files, employee tax documents, and various financial documents. The group set a four-day deadline for its unspecified ransom demand to be met, threatening to otherwise offer the data for sale for 10 Bitcoin (around $1,150,000).

The Devman hacking group targeted Thailand's Ministry of Labour, defacing its website and allegedly stealing 300 GB of data, including citizen data, information on foreign visitors, and classified documents. They demanded a €13 million ransom, claiming to have been active in the organization's directory and Linux servers for more than 43 days, encrypting 2,000 laptops and dozens of servers. The incident was reported by Thai officials on 17 July 2025, after they restored the Ministry of Labour website.

Title (Company): United Australia Party (UAP) - Trumpet of Patriots Party
Description: On 23 June 2025, the United Australia Party (UAP) and Clive Palmer's Trumpet of Patriots party were victims of a ransomware attack, resulting in unauthorized access to their servers and potential exfiltration of certain data records, including email correspondence and documents. The UAP confirmed the breach on their website on 17 July 2025, stating that they were unable to confirm what specific data was compromised and would not be notifying affected members or site visitors due to impracticality.

Between March and June 2025, at least three China-aligned hacking groups (UNK_SparkyCarp, UNK_DropPitch, UNK_FistBump) conducted targeted cyber espionage operations against Taiwan's semiconductor companies and financial analysts, with the activities believed to ongoing in July 2025. The victims, ranging from small firms to multinational companies and investment analysts, including some at a US-based global bank, were targeted by various methods. Among them were spoofed university email accounts posing as jobseekers sending infected files, and fake investment firms luring analysts with malware-laced documents. The attacks, which coincided with growing US restrictions on chip exports to China, were reported by cybersecurity firm Proofpoint on 17 July 2025.

In late 2024, threat activity tracked by Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 team as CLSTA1020 targeted government entities in Southeast Asia. The attackers collected and attempted to exfiltrate sensitive data, including information related to tariffs and trade disputes. They deployed a previously undocumented Windows backdoor, dubbed HazyBeacon, which leveraged AWS Lambda URLs for command and control (C2) communication, enabling the malware to blend with legitimate AWS traffic and evade detection. HazyBeacon, disguised as mscorsvc.dll, was sideloaded by a legitimate Windows executable and established a covert C2 channel. Once active, it received commands and downloaded additional payloads. The attackers attempted to exfiltrate files using tools such as GoogleGet.exe, uploading to Google Drive and Dropbox, though these attempts were blocked by detection mechanisms. Cleanup commands were later issued to remove traces of the intrusion.

Between March and December 2024, the China-linked APT group Salt Typhoon breached a US state's Army National Guard network, exploiting known vulnerabilities and using leased IP addresses to mask its activity. The group exfiltrated administrator credentials, network diagrams, and traffic data exchanged with National Guard units across all US states and at least four territories. Stolen data also included personally identifiable information (PII) and a map of service member locations, potentially enabling future targeted intrusions and weakening state-level cyber defences.

On 13 July 2025, Seoul Guarantee Insurance (SGI), Korea’s largest comprehensive guarantee insurance provider, confirmed it was recovering from a ransomware attack attributed to an unidentified threat actor. The attack had disrupted core systems, affecting key services such as the issuance and verification of guarantee insurance policies. SGI stated that no direct communication was established with the threat actor, and no ransom demand was received. The firm launched a response effort led by senior leadership, with support from financial security authorities, oil pipeline infrastructure teams, and other relevant stakeholders. SGI worked closely with financial administrators and security officers to restore services and assess damage. Core operations were reportedly restored by 17 July. The Financial Services Commission and the Financial Supervisory Service have launched an investigation into the incident and are reviewing potential legal or regulatory gaps. SGI pledged to fully compensate verified losses.

North Korea-linked threat actors, tied to an ongoing supply chain attack dubbed "Contagious Interview," planted 67 malicious packages in a Node Package Manager (npm) online repository since at least April 2025, delivering a new malware loader called XORIndex to developer systems. npm is the standard package manager for Node.js, a platform used by developers to share and source JavaScript libraries and tools. The packages (which deployed XORIndex and another loader known as HexEval), which together counted more than 17,000 downloads, were discovered by researchers at package security platform Socket, which reported on them on 15 July 2025.  According to the Socket report, when victims installed any of these packages, a post-install script executed to launch XORIndex Loader, which collected host data and sent it to a hardcoded command and control (C2) address hosted by the cloud application company Vercel, consistent with the use of legitimate infrastructure providers previously observed for Contagious Interview. The C2 server responded with one or more JavaScript payloads, typically the BeaverTail and InvisibleFerret backdoors, which provided access to compromised machines, allowed data exfiltration and downloaded more payloads. The North Korean hackers blended old and new tools with subtle modifications to evade detection, rotating through new npm maintainer aliases, reusing loaders like HexEval Loader, and actively deploying newly observed variants including XORIndex Loader.
Techniques Used: Automated Exfiltration, Exfiltration Over C2 Channel

Description: Unknown hackers compromised several employee email accounts related to the district administration office Odenwaldkreis in the German state of Hesse through a phishing attack on 10 July 2025. Staff were tricked into entering their credentials on a fraudulent website designed to imitate an official login page. While multiple accounts were accessed and subsequently misused, the broader IT infrastructure remained unaffected and no citizen data was compromised. The IT department immediately responded by blocking the impacted accounts, disconnecting affected systems, and launching a diagnostic review of around 40 employee accounts. The administration is working with the Hessian Ministry of the Interior’s Cyber Competence Centre to investigate the incident, which is believed to be part of a larger phishing campaign.

The Federal University of Piauí (UFPI) in Brazil suffered an intrusion severely disrupting several institutional services, including Gitsig, Sinapse, and GIS systems. The incident began around 2:30 p.m. on 12 July 2025, when technical teams observed system crashes caused by resource exhaustion and full storage on backup servers. Although initially treated as a technical malfunction, further investigation revealed the presence of malicious scripts on infrastructure machines.  Despite emergency interventions such as forced reboots, firewall blocks, and machine cloning, the university was unable to fully restore services. As of 13 July, systems remained unstable.

Suspected Chinese hackers breached the email accounts of attorneys and advisers at the Washington, DC law firm Wiley Rein in an apparent intelligence-gathering operation. The hackers, believed to be affiliated with the Chinese government, targeted information related to trade, Taiwan, and US government agencies involved in setting tariffs and reviewing foreign investment. They accessed messages in the Microsoft 365 accounts of certain Wiley personnel for intelligence gathering purposes. CNN reported on this incident, which was disclosed by Wiley Rein to its clients in a memo, on 12 July 2025.

On 10 June 2025, Albemarle County in Virginia was subject to a ransomware attack, resulting in the compromise of personal information of residents, including driving licence numbers, Social Security numbers, passport numbers, military IDs, names, addresses, and Social Security numbers. The incident was discovered on 11 June 2025, and officials from the county, the FBI, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), and the Cyber Fusion Center of the Virginia State Police were notified. The threat actor failed to gain access to cloud-based systems but breached data held on local servers. Phone services were restored after a two-week outage. Emergency phone lines were unaffected.

On 19 June 2025, the cybercriminal group Sarcoma claimed responsibility for a ransomware attack on the Zurich public health foundation Radix, allegedly stealing around two terabytes of sensitive data. Radix is a Zurich-based non-profit organization dedicated to health promotion. The Swiss government confirmed that Radix’s customers include various federal offices that might also be affected. The attackers published screenshots of allegedly stolen documents. The exact nature of the compromised information remains unclear. In the end of June 2025, the hackers published the data on the dark web.

On 10 July 2025, a pro-Russian hacker group named NoName057(16) launched a Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack on the state portal of Saxony-Anhalt, Germany, making several ministry websites temporarily inaccessible for a few hours. The attack was confirmed by a spokesperson for the Digital Ministry of the state, who informed the news agency dpa. The IT service provider Dataport, which also serves the public administration in Hamburg, Bremen, and Schleswig-Holstein, reported no disruptions in these regions. From 14 to 17 July 2025, an international law enforcement operation code-named Eastwood was launched against NoName057(16). Coordinated by Europol and Eurojust, the operation involved simultaneous actions by authorities in Czechia, France, Finland, Germany, Italy, Lithuania, Poland, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, the Netherlands, and the United States, targeting individuals and digital infrastructure linked to the pro-Russian network. Operation Eastwood allowed for the deactivation of several hundred servers supporting the group’s DDoS activities. Overall, national authorities issued seven arrest warrants, including against six Russian nationals, over the suspected involvement in NoName057(16). The investigation further facilitated the arrest of two individuals in France and Spain. Law enforcement personally notified over 1,000 supporters of the group, including 15 suspected administrators, of their legal liability related to the participation in NoName057(16)‘s criminal activities.

On 30 June 2025, the French semiconductor company Semco Technologies discovered a compromise by the Russian-speaking cybercriminal group Qilin. The company confirmed the breach on 7 July, during the final phase of the subscription period for its initial public offering. Despite the intrusion, the company’s share price surged 41% on its first day of trading debut on 9 July 2025. Qilin claimed responsibility and published stolen employee data online, including passports and invoices, likely seeking financial gain.

On 9 July 2025, an unknown hacker exploited a vulnerability in the decentralized cryptocurrency exchange GMX, stealing over $40 million in assets. The platform confirmed the breach via social media and launched an investigation. Blockchain security firms tracked approximately $43 million in user funds withdrawn and laundered into Ethereum, USD Coin, and the Ethereum-based stablecoin token DAI. GMX disabled trading and offered the attacker a 10% bounty in exchange for returning the rest, promising no legal action if the funds were returned within 48 hours.

On 7 March 2025, Nippon Steel Solutions, a subsidiary of Japan’s Nippon Steel, suffered a cyberattack after hackers exploited a zero-day vulnerability in unspecified parts of the company’s network equipment. The breach led to unauthorized access and potential exposure of personal data belonging to customers, partners, and employees. Compromised data included names, job titles, email addresses, phone numbers, and company affiliations. The company isolated the affected servers, consulted with external experts, and took corrective actions including system reconstruction and enhanced network monitoring. While there was no evidence of data being leaked online, Nippon Steel Solutions notified affected individuals, reported the incident to authorities and advised caution against potential phishing attempts.

The website of the German city of Nuremberg was targeted by a DDoS attack, disrupting access to its online services, authority guide and contact forms on 9 July 2025. City officials stated that no citizen data was compromised and that the attack originated externally. This marked the second such incident, following a similar attack in April. While updated security measures were still being implemented, the city filed a criminal complaint and involved the cybercrime unit of the Nuremberg police. The pro-Russian hacker group NoName057(16) is suspected of being responsible for the attack, according to the spokesperson for the Central Cybercrime Office at the Bamberg Public Prosecutor's Office. From 14 to 17 July 2025, an international law enforcement operation code-named Eastwood was launched against NoName057(16). Coordinated by Europol and Eurojust, the operation involved simultaneous actions by authorities in Czechia, France, Finland, Germany, Italy, Lithuania, Poland, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, the Netherlands, and the United States, targeting individuals and digital infrastructure linked to the pro-Russian network. Operation Eastwood allowed for the deactivation of several hundred servers supporting the group’s DDoS activities. Overall, national authorities issued seven arrest warrants, including against six Russian nationals, over the suspected involvement in NoName057(16). The investigation further facilitated the arrest of two individuals in France and Spain. Law enforcement personally notified over 1,000 supporters of the group, including 15 suspected administrators, of their legal liability related to the participation in NoName057(16)‘s criminal activities.

The hacktivist group Cyber Support Front carried out a cyberattack on a food production facility certified by the Israeli Ministry of Defense and army as a military supplier in early July 2025. The attack disabled the factory’s production lines and compromised its food safety database, potentially endangering the health of Israeli military personnel. The group claimed responsibility for the operation. On the same day, reports surfaced confirming the incident. In a related campaign the previous week, the Cyber Support Front also targeted two factories in the occupied Palestinian territories involved in military component manufacturing, exfiltrating over 6 TB of sensitive and classified information.

Deer Oaks Behavioral Health in Texas was breached by the ransomware group LockBit on 29 August 2023. The compromise affected information of 171,871 patients, including their names, addresses, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, diagnosis codes, insurance information, and treatment service types. On 7 July 2025, Deer Oaks reached an agreement to settle an investigation by the US Department of Health and Human Services' Office for Civil Rights (OCR) into the health providers security practices following the LockBit breach and an earlier inadvertent data leak. From at least December 2021 until 19 May 2023, a coding error in an online patient portal pilot program had exposed electronic protected health information (ePHI) of 35 individuals publicly on the internet. The OCR investigation concluded that during the time of the incidents Deer Oaks failed to conduct an accurate risk analysis and impermissibly disclosed ePHI. As a result of the investigation, Deer Oaks agreed to implement a corrective action plan, pay $225,000 to OCR, and conduct annual reviews and updates of its risk analysis, develop a risk management plan, and provide annual training for workforce members on policies and procedures required under the US Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA).

Title (Company): City Council of Villajoyosa - Local Police of Villajoyosa
Description: The City Council of Villajoyosa suffered a ransomware attack, which was detected on 2 July 2025. The Council confirmed the detection of anomalous activity and ransomware artefacts on municipal computer systems in a press statement the following day. The disruptions affected the computer systems of the local police and other municipal services, with mitigation efforts expected to last for several days.

The Anatsa Android banking trojan was used to target North American bank customers, specifically in the United States and Canada. The malware was embedded in a seemingly harmless file reader app on the Google Play Store. The app, which had amassed over 50,000 downloads, was updated with malicious code between 24 and 30 June 2025, enabling the logging keystrokes, theft of banking credentials, and initiation of fraudulent transactions. ThreatFabric researchers, who have been monitoring Anatsa's activity since 2020, reported the campaign to Google, which subsequently removed the malicious app from the store.

A previously undocumented spyware campaign tracked as 'Batavia' targeted dozens of Russian organizations, primarily large industrial enterprises, from at least July 2024 to February 2025. According to Kaspersky, more than 100 users across several dozen organizations were affected. The threat actors used phishing emails with contract-related lures that contained links to malicious archives with Visual Basic Encoded script (.VBE) files. When executed, the script profiled the host system and sent details to the command and control server (C2), then downloaded the next stage payload.

On 7 June 2025, an espionage operation was detected which was carried out by the Pakistan-based group Transparent Tribe (aka APT36), targeting Indian defence personnel and organizations that used BOSS Linux, an Indian Linux distribution. The threat actor employed phishing emails with compressed files, typically ZIP archives named CyberSecurityAdvisory.zip, containing a malicious desktop file. When opened, this file created a diversion by displaying a normal-looking PowerPoint file while secretly downloading and running another malicious program, BOSS.elf, saved locally as client.elf, which attempted to connect to a control server. The activities were first reported on 8 July 2025 and attributed by IT security company Cyfirma.

Unidentified hackers breached the servers of Russian developers responsible for distributing custom firmware, known as 1001, used to convert consumer drones for military use in Ukraine, 'Russian Hackers for the Front', the developers behind the hardware program, disclosed on 7 July 2025. The developers claim around 200,000 drones had been updated with the 1001 firmware by March 2025. The threat actors displayed false messages on operator terminals and then disabled the system, disrupting the distribution of the software. The firmware itself was not compromised, according to the developers.

A hacktivist breached Columbia University's IT systems before 24 June 2025, stealing 1.6 gigabyte of data, comprising student information from 2.5 million applications, including citizenship status, university ID numbers, admission and financial aid decisions, academic programs applied for, as well as details on employee pay and at least 1.8 million Social Security numbers. According to media reports, the hacktivist selected data in line with not further specified political goals. In a statement on the incident on 1 July 2025, Columbia University also noted disruptions to certain IT systems as a result of the intrusion.

Unknown hackers stole sensitive files from the Private Hospital of the Loire (HPL) in July 2025, compromising patient data including names, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, and contact information. The hospital filed a complaint and notified the National Commission for Information Technology and Freedoms (CNIL). On 10 July 2025, the hospital started to inform more than 126,000 patients affected by the hack. On 12 July 2025, an individual hacker named 'Marak' claimed responsibility for the incident and said that they no longer intended to sell or leak the stolen data.

A suspected ransomware attack occurred on West Lothian Council Schools' education network on 6 May 2025, located in Scotland. The attack was claimed by a ransomware gang called Interlock, though the exact circumstances and impact of the attack are yet unclear as an investigation continues. In the meantime, the West Lothian Council's IT staff worked to resolve the issue and mitigate the impact, with contingency plans allowing schools to continue operating with minimal disruption. The attack was contained to the education network, which was subsequently isolated from the rest of the Council's networks in order to minimize damage. Despite the uncertainty surrounding the incident, the Council stated on 15 July 2025 that a "small percentage of the total data stored on our Education Network has been compromised" and that a "small amount of information held by a number of our secondary schools, and one primary school, was compromised" as part of the incident, with a small amount of the data being of a not further specified personal and sensitive nature.

On 1 July 2025, food producer Hero España suffered an intrusion on its computer systems at the Sewer plant in Alcantarilla, Spain, which temporarily limited the company's productive and logistic activity. The unidentified threat actors prompted the company to shut down affected systems to prevent further unauthorized access and protect information. Hero activated contingency plans to mitigate the impact on customers and partners, with no effect on other international subsidiaries of the Hero Group. The company informed the public about the incident through a statement, emphasizing the security of employees, customers, and data as their top priority.

On 27 June 2025, Varonis researchers reported that at least one threat actor was exploiting a Microsoft Exchange Online feature called Direct Send to send phishing emails to Microsoft 365 tenants and their employees. The attacker used a PowerShell script to assemble the phishing emails and sent them to the Direct Send endpoint, which allowed the emails to be delivered without authentication or SPF, DKIM, or DMARC checks. Since May 2025, the campaign targeted over 70 organizations in various sectors including finance and health, mostly in the US.
Techniques Used: Exploit Public-Facing Application, Hardware Additions, Phishing

Description: On 22 April 2025, BlackSuit hackers breached the systems of Gloucester County in Virginia, exposing Social Security numbers and other sensitive data of government employees, including names, drivers license numbers, bank account information, health insurance numbers, and medical information. The county administrator, Carol Steele, hired cybersecurity experts to aid in recovery and notified the FBI's Cyber Crimes Division and the Cyber Fusion Center of the Virginia State Police. The county initially reported network disruptions on 22 and 23 April but did not provide further updates until sending notices to affected employees in July. The BlackSuit ransomware gang claimed responsibility for the attack on 15 May stating that the county refused to negotiate a ransom. On 24 Jul 2025, BlackSuit’s technical infrastructure was seized in a globally coordinated takedown.

On 1 July 2025, the hacker group CyberTeam targeted the website of Infocheck service, an offering for customers of the credit reporting company Equifax S.A. in Paraguay. Infocheck also manages the Informconf credit information service. CyberTeam claimed to have temporarily knocked the website offline.

On 30 June 2025, hackers breached C&M Software, a tech company authorized by Brazil's central bank to connect smaller banks and fintech companies to national banking systems, in particular the instant payment system PIX operated by the central bank. The threat actors used login credentials acquired from C&M employee João Roque for about 2,700 Brazilian reais (around $500), enabling them to initiate fraudulent PIX transactions. They accessed reserve accounts and stole over 800 million reais ($140 million) from six financial institutions, including BMP, Credsystem, and Banco Paulista. Roughly 30 to 40 million reais were converted into the cryptocurrencies Bitcoin, Ether, and Tether, then laundered via Latin American exchanges and over-the-counter trading (OTC) platforms. Brazil's central bank suspended access to C&M Software’s systems to contain damage. Roque was arrested and investigations continue to recover funds and identify others involved.

Qantas, an Australian airline, was targeted on 20 June 2025, when threat actors gained access to a third-party call center platform, containing data of six million customers including customer names, email addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, and frequent flying numbers. The breach was discovered on 30 June 2025 and contained by 2 July 2025. Cybersecurity analysts warn that this intrusion fits the pattern of the hacking group Scattered Spider that has hit multiple airlines in recent weeks. Qantas worked with the Australian Cyber Security Centre and privacy regulators to investigate the breach. Affected customers were contacted directly, and the airline recommended that passengers stay alert for phishing emails pretending to be from Qantas.

On 30 June 2025, an unidentified hacker group launched a ransomware attack on the Adige Po reclamation consortium in Italy, which manages the network of canals and water pumps in the region. The breach was promptly identified and contained by in-house technicians with support from external cybersecurity experts brought in to neutralize the threat. While the incident led to the encryption and theft of some digital files and archives, it did not disrupt the operation of control units or water pumps in the field. Consortium President Roberto Branco and General Manager Marco Volpin confirmed the incident.

In late June or early July 2025, the private Telegram account of Lee Beom-Seok, the major of the South Korean city of Cheongju, was hacked. The attackers sent request messages to citizens and administrators, attempting to solicit money under false pretenses. The Cheongju City Secretary’s Office issued an emergency notice in response, warning against responding to these demands. To mitigate further damage, city officials informed reporters, foreign agencies, and the police about the incident.

The International Criminal Court (ICC) was compromised in a network intrusion detected and contained during the last week of June 2025, the ICC disclosed in a press statement on 30 June 2025. The ICC's alert and response mechanisms enabled swift discovery, confirmation, and containment of the breach. The ICC is conducting a Court-wide impact analysis to assess the extent of the incident and implementing steps to mitigate any effects resulting from the compromise.

Not further specified North Korean hackers were connected to a compromise of various NFT projects, including ChainSaw and Favrr, which started on 18 June 2025, and was revealed by crypto investigator ZachXBT on 27 June 2025. The attackers took over NFT contracts, made a profit by mass-producing and dumping NFTs in the market, and stole approximately $1 million from the projects. ZachXBT attributed the activity to a cluster of North Korean IT workers that had unwittingly been hired for the development of the NFT projects.

On 27 June 2025, the Institute of Public Health (ISP) of Chile, a certification body and national drug agency of the country, experienced a network intrusion. In response, the institute's servers were taken offline to avoid any data leak and the National Cybersecurity Agency (ANCI) was informed on the same day. One week after the incident was detected, the institute gradually began reconnecting its systems and reactivated its integration into the citizen information portal SIAC.

The China-linked threat group Hive0154 was observed by IBM X-Force to be distributing Pubload malware through an ongoing phishing campaign targeting the Tibetan community in the lead-up to events centring around the Dalai Lama's 90th birthday (in July 2025) and the 9th World Parliamentarians' Convention on Tibet (WPCT), which occurred in June 2025. To further the campaign, Hive0154 used both legitimate and malicious files within their phishing lures, copying legitimate texts/articles and embedding malware into certain other files, such as DOCX files, in an attempt to make the victim trust the legitimacy of the emails sent.

Title (Company): Unified Portal for Access to Public Public Information
Description: On 26 June 2025, cybercriminals linked to the CyberTeam collective defaced the website of the Unified Portal for Access to Public Public Information of Paraguay, a civil service body under the Paraguayan government responsible for disseminating public records when requested. The group allegedly gained control over website content through stolen credentials. The incident, for which CyberTeam claimed responsibility on social media, was confirmed by Diana Valdez, director of the Cyber Incident Response Center at the Ministry of Information and Communication Technologies (MITIC), who explained that the breach occurred due to the leaking of one of the passwords of a system responder.

Hawaiian Airlines was breached in a cyber incident that disrupted access to some of its systems on or around 26 June 2025, with several anonymous sources claiming that the incident was the work of Scattered Spider; one anonymous source who spoke to Reuters about Scattered Spider's involvement had worked to mitigate several other Scattered Spider incidents in the past. An FBI warning about the group targeting the airline sector aligning with this assessment. Reporting by Palo Alto Networks indicated further circumstantial evidence for this attack pattern. The airline hired external cybersecurity experts to assess the incident's impact and restore affected systems. Hawaiian Airlines informed the public about the breach through a statement on their website and a banner noting that flights were not impacted. The Federal Aviation Administration also commented on the incident, stating that there was no impact on safety and that the airline continued to operate safely.

Iran-linked Educated Manticore launched a phishing campaign targeting Israeli journalists, cybersecurity professionals, and computer science professors in June 2025, coinciding with the outbreak of the Iran-Israel war. The threat actors posed as employees of cybersecurity firms, using emails and WhatsApp messages to trick victims into revealing their email credentials and two-factor authentication codes. The phishing messages were crafted with AI assistance and initially contained no links, but later directed victims to phishing links disguised as Google Meet invitations or Gmail login pages. Israeli cyber and computer science experts were among those targeted. The campaign was disclosed by Checkpoint Research on 25 June 2025, which assesses Educated Manticore to operate under instructions of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ Intelligence Organization (IRGC-IO).

Netspeed, a leading Internet service provider (ISP) in Türkiye, was targeted in efforts to disrupt its services which started on 24 June 2025 and lasted for three days. The activities caused communication cut-offs, resulting in subscribers being unable to access the internet and the company's call centre being unreachable. Netspeed disclosed the incident through a statement on social media on 27 June 2025, stating that technical teams were working around the clock to resolve the issue and that necessary measures had been taken to restore services to normal. Netspeed's statement did not provide information on whether the disruptions were the result of a network compromise.

China-nexus hackers, linked to an APT known as UAT-5918, hijacked over 1,000 SOHO devices in a continuous espionage campaign tracked as "LapDogs," which started at least in September 2023 and was discovered by SecurityScorecards STRIKE team that disclosed the activities on 23 June 2025. The threat actors used a Linux-based ShortLeash malware sample and its startup Bash script to form a covert network, called an Operational Relay Box (ORB), to support long-term spying operations. The malware targeted a wide range of hardware and firmware vendors, including ASUS, D-Link, Microsoft, Panasonic, Synology, and more, with systems running services like GoAhead web apps, WRT admin panels, and IIS being especially at risk. The threat actors exploited known flaws like CVE-2015-1548 and CVE-2017-17663, linked to outdated mini-httpd servers. The LapDogs campaign showed targeted behaviour, with most certificates within a group being generated just 1.8 seconds apart, demonstrating automated attacks rather than manual infections. The attackers favoured certain countries and regions, especially the US and Southeast Asia, and many intrusion sets centred around specific locations, showing careful planning and long-term goals. Cisco Talos, which has tracked UAT-5918 activity going back to at least 2023, observed overlaps between the group's post-compromise activity, TTPs, as well as targeted verticals with Volt Typhoon, Flax Typhoon, Earth Estries, and Dalbit.

Title (Company): Firefighters Station of the Permanent Corps of Bolzano - Provincial Operations Centre of the South Tyrol Health Agency - Provincial Radio Communications Service of the Civil Protection Agency - Provincial Road Station
Description: On 23 June 2025, a cyber attack was carried out on the Province of Bolzano, specifically targeting systems of the Provincial Operations Centre of the South Tyrol Health Agency, the Provincial Road Station, the Firefighters Station of the Permanent Corps of Bolzano, and the Provincial Radio Communications Service of the Civil Protection Agency. The threat actors used malware to compromise the system, with the cause of the failure known by 25 June 2025. Forensic analysis was ongoing as of 26 June 2025. The Province reported that restoration efforts began on 26 June 2025, and were expected to be completed in the next few days without interruption. Despite the incident, emergency services remained operational, with staff working manually to receive telephone calls and radio communications. The provincial radio network was largely unaffected, with over 130 out of 140 Tetra network stations remaining active. The Province stated that the damage was limited to a single system and did not spread, ensuring all Agency services continued to function, albeit with some short-term limitations.

On 29 June 2025, Glasgow City Council was hit by a cyber attack, potentially resulting in the theft of customer data. The Council's services were taken offline, including planning applications, payment of parking or bus lane fines, and ordering certificates, after malicious activity was detected on servers managed by a third-party supplier. The incident did not involve email, and email communication with the Council remained safe. The affected services included planning, penalty charge notices, pensions, registrars, revenues and benefits as well as several online forms for citizens to submit permit and certificate applications, complaints, and FOI requests. The Council, alongside police and the national and Scottish cyber security centres, investigated the incident and advised individuals who had used the affected forms to be cautious about any contact claiming to be from the Council.

Title (Company): Civil Hospitals of Guadalajara - DIF Guadalajara
Description: On 24 June 2025, a cyber attack was carried out against the DIF Guadalajara system and the Civil Hospitals of Guadalajara in Mexico, compromising personal data of its users. The exact number of people affected has not been determined, but it is reported that over 33,000 files containing personal, medical, financial, and employment data of patients and workers were stolen from the hospital. A hacker operating under the pseudonym 'Kazu' claimed responsibility for the breach and offered to sell a cache of 7.6 GB of stolen date for $250. The University of Guadalajara and DIF Guadalajara reported that they had filed complaints with the relevant authorities and strengthened cybersecurity measures to protect user data. The same threat actor is suspected to also have compromised the Guadalajara DIF System, exposing data from over 63,000 people.

Title (Company): Education Council of Castile and León
Description: A student breached the information systems of the Education Council of Castile and León's in Spain on 31 May 2025, compromising the personal data of thousands of students and their families. The compromise, which was detected on 31 May and confirmed on 2 June, gave the hacker access to personal information including names, identity cards, addresses, telephones, emails, and birthdates. The Education Department implemented technical measures to block the attack, strengthened management applications, and incorporated new filters and monitoring alerts. The incident was notified to the Spanish Data Protection Agency and a formal complaint was filed with the Civil Guard. The incident was reported by various sources, including Carlos Fernández Carriedo, the Minister of Economy and Finance, who stated that the student had usurped a teacher's identity and access key. In statements posted under the handle 'MafiaTributaria', the student claimed to have obtained a database containing over a million personal records of students and their parents.  The Socialist Parliamentary Group raised the incident, criticizing that the event had not disclosed in the plenary of the Courts of Castile and León.

On 10 April 2024, The Inc Ransom group breached the network of Mainline Health Systems, a healthcare organization, impacting 101,104 individuals. The attackers gained unauthorized access to certain files containing protected personal information. Mainline Health Systems disclosed the data breach on 21 May 2025, after conducting a thorough investigation with external cybersecurity experts and notifying federal law enforcement. The Inc Ransom Group claimed responsibility for the incident and added the organization to its Tor leak site on 29 April 2025.

Pro-Russian hacking group Z-Pentest breached the control systems of a Norwegian dam at Lake Risevatnet near the city of Svelgen in southwest Norway in April 2025, opening its water valve at full capacity for four hours before the intrusion was detected. The incident, reported by Norwegian energy news outlet Energiteknikk on 25 June 2025, was discovered on 7 April by the dam’s owner, Breivika Eiendom. Norwegian authorities, including the NSM (National Security Authority), NVE (Norwegian Water Resources and Energy Directorate), and Kripos (a special agency of the Norwegian Police Service), were notified on 10 April. Officials believe the attackers exploited a weak password protecting the valve’s web-accessible control panel, a vulnerability identified by Breivika technical manager Bjarte Steinhovden. The hackers’ actions did not endanger the public, as the water flow only slightly exceeded the dam’s minimum discharge requirement. In August 2025, Z-Pentest released a video showing operatives taking control of the dam thereby claiming responsibility for the attack. Norwegian officials attributed the attack to pro-Russian hackers without specifically mentioning the threat actor.

On 20 August 2023, the BlackCat (AlphV) ransomware gang attacked MNGI Digestive Health, a multilocation gastroenterology practice in Minnesota, and exfiltrated over 2 TB of files, including patient information such as full names, dates of birth, passport numbers, driver’s license or state identification numbers, medical information, health insurance information, payment card information, account numbers, and Social Security numbers. The incident was discovered by MNGI on 25 August 2023, and first reported on DataBreaches on 25 September 2023. BlackCat posted diatribes on its dark web leak site and leaked over 800 GB of data after MNGI did not pay, threatening further data leakage, spam, and harassment. The breach affected 767,670 patients, as reported to HHS in October 2023. Individual notification letters were sent out in July 2024. The attack was claimed by the BlackCat (AlphV) ransomware gang. MNGI Digestive Health received court approval on 7 May 2025, to settle a class action case brought by affected patients.

On 22 June 2025, the Autonomous City of Melilla experienced a cyber attack that rendered its computer system inoperative, affecting its official website and online administrative services. The president of Melilla, Juan Jos Imbroda, reported the incident and stated that the technical services and the CNI (Spanish National Intelligence Center) are working to resolve the issue. The computer services were out of service for several days, causing significant declines in internet and telephone services, and generating concern among citizens and local authorities. On 26 June 2026, Qilin Ransomware Group released a statement claiming to have obtained four to five terrabytes of data and demanding a ransom of 1.8 million euros.

In mid-February 2025, Salt Typhoon, a Chinese state-sponsored cyber threat actor, compromised three network devices registered to a Canadian telecommunications company by exploiting the CVE-2023-20198 vulnerability in Cisco IOS XE. The actors retrieved running configuration files from all three devices and modified at least one file to configure a GRE tunnel, enabling traffic collection from the network. The incident was reported and attributed by the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security and the FBI on 19 June 2025.

Iran-linked threat actors, associated with the Cyber Fattah movement, leaked thousands of records containing information about visitors and athletes from past Saudi Games on 22 June 2025. The attackers gained unauthorized access to phpMyAdmin and exfiltrated stored records in the form of SQL dumps. The stolen data originated from a database related to the Saudi Games 2024 official website, where visitors, athletes, and their teams could register and share personal information. The breach contained sensitive data, including personally identifiable information (PII), International Bank Account Numbers (IBANs), and medical examination certificates. US-based cybersecurity firm Resecurity identified the threat actors and reported the incident.

A hacker targeted the Ukrainian Web3 security auditing company Hacken, compromising the private key associated with the bridge deployment that allowed them to create 900 million HAI tokens on the Ethereum and BNB Chain networks on 21 June 2025. The incident resulted in a 98% collapse in the value of HAI, with the hacker selling tokens worth over $250,000. Hacken confirmed the unauthorized minting of HAI tokens on Ethereum and BNB Chain and said it was not a hack, but a human error during architectural changes.

The Russian state-sponsored threat group APT28, also tracked as UAC-0001, launched malware attacks on government targets in Ukraine via Signal chats. The attacks were first discovered by Ukraine's Computer and Emergency Response (CERT-UA) in March 2024. Over a year later, in May 2025, ESET notified CERT-UA of unauthorized access to a gov.ua email account. During this investigation, CERT-UA found that malicious documents (.doc) were sent via Signal, using macros to load the Covenant backdoor, which acted as a malware loader, downloading and loading previously undocumented malware families named BeardShell and SlimAgent. BeardShell downloaded PowerShell scripts, decrypted them, and executed them, with results exfiltrated to APT28's command-and-control (C2) server. SlimAgent captured screenshots using Windows API functions, encrypted them with AES and RSA, and stored them locally for potential exfiltration. CERT-UA attributes this activity to APT28.

Title (Company): Chain IQ - UBS Group AG - Geneva Pictet
Description: On 18 June 2025, Worldleaks breached the external procurement service provider Chain IQ resulted in the theft of data related to UBS Group AG and several other companies, including the private bank Geneva Pictet. Approximately 130,000 UBS employees were affected. The leaked data included names, email addresses, fixed and mobile phone numbers, hierarchical roles, spoken languages, and internal codes indicating assigned locations and plans. No customer data were involved.

Systems of the Oxford City Council were breached over the weekend of 7–8 June 2025, resulting in potential unauthorised access to personal information of Council staff involved in election duties between 2001 and 2022. The Council’s automated security systems detected and removed the intrusion early, limiting access to systems and databases. While precautionary measures led to some service disruptions, email and digital platforms remained secure.
