The town immediately launched an investigation, engaged the services of the North Carolina Joint Cybersecurity Task Force, and reported the incident to federal law enforcement. The town has been working to restore systems in a secure manner and has made significant progress, but the incident response process has required extensive time, labor, and resources. The town has also been providing updates on the incident and has informed the public that emergency services were not interrupted and remained operational throughout the incident

Title (Company): Not available - Not available - Not available - Not available - Not available - Not available - Not available
Description: Bitdefender Labs has identified an ongoing cyber-espionage campaign orchestrated by the threat actor UAC-0063 targeting organizations in Central Asia and Europe. Initially focused on government institutions in Central Asia, the group has expanded its operations to include embassies in Germany, the UK, the Netherlands, Romania, and Georgia, aiming to exfiltrate sensitive data from high-value targets.  The attackers gained initial access by weaponizing stolen Microsoft Word documents from previously compromised victims, exemplifying a supply chain attack strategy. These malicious documents deployrf the HATVIBE loader and other malware, including DownEx, DownExPyer (also known as CHERRYSPY), and PyPlunderPlug, a USB-based data exfiltrator. To evade detection, the attackers delivered the weaponized documents via phishing emails that contain download links rather than direct attachments. Upon opening the documents, users encountered blurred pages and misleading warnings urging them to enable macros, which triggered malware execution. CERT-UA has assessed with moderate confidence that UAC-0063 is linked to the Russian cyber-espionage group APT28 (BlueDelta). Still, no definitive technical evidence existed to confirm this connection for Bitdefender Labs.  In September and October 2024, multiple alerts detected weaponized documents uploaded from Kazakhstan likely exfiltrated from Kazakh embassies based on metadata. On November 21, 2024, the latest attack attempt involved a malicious document hosted on a compromised server, which was sent via phishing emails. On April 4, 2024, a newly compiled version of DownExPyer was deployed against a target in Romania, while on January 12, 2023, the PyPlunderPlug USB exfiltration tool was found on a compromised system in Germany.
Techniques Used: Automated Exfiltration, Drive-by Compromise, Phishing, Valid Accounts

Description: On 28 January 2025, the strassen.gr.ch website, run by the Civil Engineering Office of the Canton of Graubünden in Switzerland, was the victim of a cyber attack. The attack occurred between 10:00 and 15:30, making road map data inaccessible.

On 15 November 2019, the Rouen University Hospital Centre was targeted by a large-scale cyberattack. The IT department noticed the encryption of their data at 7 p.m.. A ransom request was made by the Russian Hackers Community, but the hospital refused to pay. The medical center recovered all access in less than two weeks without any data leak.  Rémi Heym, director of communication at the hospital, reported the incident, which was published by 'Paris Normandie' on 28 January 2025.

Title (Company): General Directorate of Civil Registry, Identification and Certification - DIGERCIC (Ecuador)
Description: The General Directorate of Civil Registry, Identification and Certification of Ecuador (DIGERCIC) was targeted in what appeared to be a DDoS attack originating from IP addresses in Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia, which affected access to online services, including the appointment scheduling system for issuing identigy cards and passports.  The institution filed a complaint with the Pichincha Prosecutors Office on 28 January 2025, to investigate the incident and establish the responsibilities of the perpetrators and accomplices.

Ukraine Military Intelligence service HUR disrupted Russian telecommunication provider MegaFon on 25 January 2025. Sources from the HUR told Kyiv Post that this was done through a DDoS attack. Disruptions were also noted for other operators, namely Yota and NetByNet and also acknowledged by Russian communication agency, Roskomnadzor.

The South African Weather Service was targeted by cybercriminals over two days, resulting in the disruption of its email system and website. The attack occurred on Saturday and Sunday, with the ICT systems going down on Sunday evening.

Title (Company): Geological Survey (Estonia) - Consumer Protection and Technical Regulatory Authority (Estonia) - Maritime Administration (Estonia) - Ministries of Economic Affairs and Communications (Estonia) - Transport Administration (Estonia)
Description: On December 1, 2020, Estonia’s Information System Authority (RIA) reported that the systems of three government ministries, including the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Ministry of Social Affairs, had been breached. Additionally, 350 gigabytes of data were exfiltrated from the systems of the Transport Administration, the Maritime Administration, the Geological Survey, and the Consumer Protection and Technical Regulatory Authority. They were attributed to Russia by Estonia in a press release on 5 September 2024, following a national and international investigation involving 10 countries, dubbed "Operation Toy Soldier". The investigation concluded that the attacks were 'malign and premeditated', aiming to damage national computer systems, obtain sensitive information, and strike a blow against Estonia's sense of security. The attacks were part of a broader campaign that also targeted Ukraine and other allies. Estonian foreign minister Margus Tsahkna and Tanel Sepp, Director General of the Cyber Diplomacy Department of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, informed the public about the attack. The US Department of Justice published an indictment alleging that GRU hackers of unit 29155 tried to gain access to Ukrainian government systems around the same time. The EU sanctioned three individuals associated with the cyber operations on 27 January 2025.

On 28 January 2025, Smiths Group, a British multinational engineering company, disclosed a security breach to the London Stock Exchange after attackers gained unauthorized access to the company's systems.  Smiths Group isolated affected systems and activated business continuity plans. The company is working with cybersecurity experts to recover affected systems and determine the impact on the business.

On 27 January 2025, a pro-Palestinian hacker group called Handala breached the emergency systems used in Israeli schools, including approximately 20 kindergartens, and broadcast rocket sirens and Arabic songs that Israel's cyber agency called supportive of terrorism. The hackers claimed to have compromised MaagarTec, an Israeli electronics firm that operates panic button systems in schools, and wiped the company's system after sending the alerts. Local media reported the incident, and the Israel National Cyber Directorate confirmed its collaboration with the company and the Ministry of Education to restore services and launched an investigation into the incident.

On 27 January 2025, Matagorda County government in Texas, serving about 40,000 residents, suffered a cyberattack that forced officials to declare a disaster. The attack, discovered on 24 January 2025, involved unauthorized access to internal systems, impacting various departments and disrupting some operations. With assistance from cybersecurity experts, the Department of Public Safety Cybersecurity Division, the Texas Department of Emergency Management, and the Department of Informational Services, the breach was contained to internal county systems. The FBI was notified of the incident. Matagorda County Judge Bobby Seiferman issued a declaration of disaster, stating the county is working to secure systems and protect sensitive information. By 27 January 2025, the county made progress in restoring some online services and placed drop boxes near the tax office for tax payments. Emergency services were not impacted.

On 17 September 2024, the ransomware gang RansomHub gained unauthorised access to the computer systems of HCF Management, a healthcare provider in the United States. The breach affected nearly 70,000 individuals. Among the impacted facilities, Heritage Health Care reported the largest breach with 12,162 affected individuals, while Hempfield Manor had the highest number of patients affected at a single location, with 4,744. HCF discovered the incident on 3 October 2024 and engaged an external forensic firm to investigate. The investigation concluded that threat actors accessed and exfiltrated data from the company's IT systems between 17 September and 3 October 2024. Exposed data may have included names, addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, medical treatment information, and health insurance details. RansomHub added HCF to its dark web leak site on 29 October 2024, claiming to have published 250 GB of stolen data. HCF formally reported the breach to federal and state regulators on 9 January 2025.

On 24 January 2025, Singapore-based cryptocurrency exchange Phemex was forced to suspend some of its operations after a suspected compromise resulted in the theft of over $69 million in crypto assets. Phemex did not immediately disclose whether a vulnerability in its security infrastructure was exploited. On 22 February, blockchain analyst ZachXBT identified an overlap in wallet addresses that linked the Lazarus Group to the incident.

On 24 January 2025, a cyber attack was carried out on the public transport passenger payment system in Tbilisi, causing it to malfunction and generate error messages, as well as play audio recordings, including the anthems of Georgia and the European Union and voice messages from politicians. The system was restored by representatives from the Bank of Georgia and Azri Ltd.

Title (Company): Topack IT Solutions GmbH - Unnamed schools in Rhineland-Palatinate
Description: On 14-15 January 2025, LockBit gained unauthorized access to the IT systems of Topack IT solutions GmbH. The provider was responsible for the IT infrastructure of at least 45 schools in Speyer, Germersheim, Bad Dürkheim, and Neustadt. LockBit 3.0 used ransomware to partially encrypt and exfiltrate data from several schools. The attackers demanded ransom in the form of cryptocurrencies to release the encrypted data, threatening to publish confidential information on the darknet if their demands were not met. By 30 January 2025, the captured data would be offered for sale. The Landeskriminalamt in Mainz and the Central Office Cybercrime of the Procuratorate General Koblenz were investigating the incident. The attack was reported on 24 January 2025.

Title (Company): Not available - Not available - Not available - Not available - IPany
Description: The PlushDaemon China-aligned hacking group breached IPany, a South Korean VPN provider, in a supply-chain attack that occurred between November 2023 and January 2025, by compromising the company's VPN installer to deploy the custom SlowStepper malware. The malware was inserted into the installer and infected customer systems when the VPN was installed. Companies impacted included a South Korean semiconductor firm and a software development company. The attack was first uncovered by ESET researchers, with the first signs of infected victims dating back to 1 November 2023 in Japan. The SlowStepper payload was loaded from a image file via a malicious DLL that was sideloaded into a PerfWatson.exe process. The particular version of SlowStepper used in these attacks was 0.2.10 Lite, which is a potent tool for extensive collection of data and spying through recording of audio and videos.

The Cuban Foreign Ministry's account on social network X was hacked on 20 January 2025. The hackers took control of the account after 08:00 local time. Any information published from the CubaMINREX account after that time was false. The Cuban Foreign Ministry denounced the hack on 20 January 2025, and warned the public about the false information through a message posted on Facebook.

On 16 January 2025, the US-American multinational information technology company Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) was informed by IntelBroker that they had stolen documents from HPE's developer environments, including source code, certificates, and personal information. IntelBroker claimed to have had access to HPE's API, WePay, and GitHub repositories for at least two days. HPE immediately launched an investigation and activated their cyber response protocols. As of 20 January 2025, HPE had not found any evidence of a security breach. The incident was reported by BleepingComputer, who was informed by HPE spokesperson Clare Loxley. IntelBroker announced the sale of the allegedly stolen information on Breach Forums, a cybercrime and data breach forum, and also shared details with Hackread.com. The stolen data included source code, private GitHub repositories, Docker builds, certificates, product source code belonging to Zerto and iLO, and user data such as old personal information related to deliveries.

Title (Company): Texas Health and Human Services Commission
Description: The Texas Health and Human Services Commission was breached by insider employees between 1 June 2021 and 31 December 2024, resulting in the improper access of personal information of at least 61,000 individuals, including full names, home addresses, telephone numbers, dates of birth, email addresses, Social Security numbers, Medicaid and Medicare Identification numbers, financial, employment, banking, benefits, health and other personal information.  The breach was discovered on 21 November 2024. The Texas Health and Human Services Commission took immediate steps to mitigate the breach, including terminating the seven employees deemed involved and referring the incident to the Texas Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General for investigation which is ongoing. Local media outlet Texas Tribune reported on the breach on 22 January 2025.

Title (Company): Government of Ebikon - Government of Adligenswil - Cantonal Bank of Zurich - Cantonal Bank of Vaud - Government of Kriens
Description: On 20 January 2025, a Russian cyber attack, claimed by the Russian group of hackers NoName057(16), affected several websites of local governments and banks in Switzerland, including the governments of three localities in Lucerne, namely Adligenswil, Kriens and Ebikon, and the cantonal banks of Zurich and Vaud, using Distributed Denial DDoS attacks. The attacks were anticipated by the Federal Office for Cyber Security due to the ongoing World Economic Forum in Davos. The Federal Office for Cyber Security reported that the hackers wanted to attract attention with this virtual demonstration online. The attacks were reported by multiple sources, including Bluewin.ch, KeystoneATS, and ATS, on Tuesday, 21 January 2025.  From 14 to 17 July 2025, an international law enforcement operation code-named Eastwood was launched against NoName057(16). Coordinated by Europol and Eurojust, the operation involved simultaneous actions by authorities in Czechia, France, Finland, Germany, Italy, Lithuania, Poland, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, the Netherlands, and the United States, targeting individuals and digital infrastructure linked to the pro-Russian network. Operation Eastwood allowed for the deactivation of several hundred servers supporting the group’s DDoS activities. Overall, national authorities issued seven arrest warrants, including against six Russian nationals, over the suspected involvement in NoName057(16). The investigation further facilitated the arrest of two individuals in France and Spain. Law enforcement personally notified over 1,000 supporters of the group, including 15 suspected administrators, of their legal liability related to the participation in NoName057(16)‘s criminal activities.

On Friday, 17 January 2025, Blacon High School in Melbourne Road, Chester, was targeted by a ransomware attack, which encrypted files and data, and demanded money in exchange for decrypting the affected system or files. The school was forced to close for two days, Monday, 20 January 2025, and Tuesday, 21 January 2025, to deal with the attack. Headteacher Rachel Hudson informed parents and carers about the incident through a statement on the school's website. An independent cybersecurity company was working to understand the extent of the attack. The school's phone systems were also affected, and alternative contact arrangements were made. The attack was reported by the school through their website, social media, and Parent Pay. Headteacher Rachel Hudson provided updates on the situation. The incident highlights the increasing frequency of cyberattacks on public sector institutions, including schools and the NHS.

Russia targeted Kazakhstan in an espionage campaign attributed to the group tracked as UAC-0063 by researchers at Sekoia. First identified by Ukrainian cyber defenders in April 2023, UAC0063 is assessed with medium confidence to overlap with APT28, linked to Unit 26165 of the Russian Main Intelligence Directorate (GRU). The campaign, revealed on 15 January 2025, involved 18 weaponized documents, including administrative notes, diplomatic letters, and intergovernmental reports. Broader regional targeting was evident, as one file originated from Kyrgyzstan's defense ministry.

LuxTrust was targeted by a Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack on Wednesday, January 15, 2025. The attack made its verification services unavailable for around half an hour, from 11:05, and was confirmed by a LuxTrust spokesperson in an email to the Luxembourg Times on the same day. This attack followed a similar DDoS attack last Friday, which disrupted several government websites and connected services, including LuxTrust, for two hours.

On 1 November 2024, unknown threat actors launched a cyberattack on Trabzon University in Turkey, seizing sensitive data belonging to 25,237 students and staff. The breach, detected on 1 June 2024, involved personal information including names, Turkish identity numbers, dates of birth, parents' names, contact details, course schedules, and institutional registration numbers. The attackers shared the stolen data on illegal platforms, prompting Trabzon University to notify all affected individuals and implement enhanced security measures. The Personal Data Protection Authority (KVKK) disclosed the breach on 16 January 2025, advising victims to remain vigilant against misuse of their information and take legal precautions. Investigations into the breach are ongoing as the university works to mitigate further risks.

Description: North Korean state-sponsored hacking group Lazarus Group compromised Web3 and virtual currency developers in numerous countries beginning on 9 January 2025 at the latest. Unveiled the same day by the SecurityScorecard STRIKE team and further detailed in a 15 January report, the campaign involved fake recruiters on platforms such as LinkedIn who tricked developers into cloning malicious GitLab repositories. These repositories infected systems with modular malware capable of keylogging, clipboard monitoring, file exfiltration, and browser credential theft. Victims were located in countries including Canada, the United States, Mexico, Brazil, Argentina, Portugal, Spain, France, the United Kingdom, Netherlands, Germany, Switzerland, Finland, Estonia, Slovakia, Ukraine, Egypt, the United Arab Emirates, Pakistan, India, Bangladesh, Thailand, Laos, Vietnam, Malaysia, Indonesia, Brunei, and South Korea with the highest number of victims in Italy. The campaign built on previous Lazarus operations but featured enhanced obfuscation, persistence, and modularity.

The Qilin Ransomware Group claimed responsibility for a cyberattack that forced the city of West Haven, Connecticut, to temporarily shut down all of its IT systems. The city initially reported a network disruption on 26 December 2024. Mayor Dorinda Borer announced the city was investigating the incident by 11 January 2025. The city's IT systems were backed up, allowing them to be operational within a few days. The city disclosed the incident to the public through a Facebook post on 26 December 2024 and an update on 11 January 2025.

On 7 December 2024, unknown perpetrators compromised the Vidymed Group, a healthcare provider with four medical centres in Lausanne and Epalinges, by breaching its information systems. The attack was detected the same day and was still ongoing in the evening. Immediate measures were taken to contain the incident and protect the integrity of the infrastructure. A crisis cell was set up due to the potential consequences on the Vaudian health system. As a result, medical records are no longer available, and the Vaud authorities called all first resort doctors and pharmacists to vigilance. The incident was reported by Vidymed in a press release on 8 December 2024.

Unknown Threat Actors breached the confidentiality of the UK internet domain registry, Nominet, by exploiting a zero-day vulnerability in the Virtual Private Network (VPN) software supplied by Ivanti, which enabled them to access systems remotely. The attack started in mid-December 2024 and was discovered by Nominet after the UK Government's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) issued an urgent bulletin encouraging organisations to mitigate vulnerabilities affecting Ivanti Connect Secure, Policy Secure, and ZTA Gateways (CVE-2025-0282 and CVE-2025-0283). ISPreview first reported the issue on January 9, 2025, after being informed by the NCSC. Nominet confirmed the attack and stated that they had no evidence of data breach or leakage, and that domain registration and management systems continued to operate as normal. The incident was reported to the relevant authorities, including the NCSC, and Nominet is working with external experts to investigate the incident and has implemented additional safeguards, including restricted access to their systems from VPN. Google Cloud also provided a detailed advisory on the vulnerabilities. On January 8, Mandiant reported on the exploitation of the same vulnerability by Chinese threat actor UNC5337, a cluster of activity assessed with moderate confidence to be part of UNC5221, also starting in Mid-December 2024. However, Mandiant reported that probably multiple actors exploit the vulnerability since then.

The government of Turks and Caicos, a British Overseas Territory with about 50,000 residents, was breached by a ransomware attack in December 2024. The attackers gained access to the government's revenue collection and payment systems, impacting numerous business operations on the islands, including government welfare payments, tax collection, and the islands' department of motor vehicles. The attack was first reported by the government on 19 December 2024, and caused significant delays in payments, including those for welfare programs, just days before Christmas. By 24 December 2024, the government confirmed that several segments of its network had been compromised. To mitigate the breach, digital applications were temporarily shut down, and most departments had to revert to manual operations. The Ministry of Finance extended the due date for tax payments and explored alternative ways to issue checks to residents and businesses. The attack was disclosed to the public by the government, and external cybersecurity specialists were engaged to aid in the recovery. The UK government covered the cost of external forensic investigators. The payment system was restored on 6 January 2025, and several other platforms were put back into operation by 8 January 2025.

Telefónica, a Spanish multinational telecommunications company, was breached by four attackers using the aliases DNA, Grep, Pryx, and Rey, who compromised an employee's credentials to access the company's internal ticketing system on 9 January 2025, and scraped approximately 2.3 GB of documents, tickets, and various data. The attackers then leaked the data on a hacking forum. The breach was reported by BleepingComputer on 10 January 2025, after being informed by Telefónica, who confirmed the incident and stated that they were investigating and had taken steps to block unauthorized access. BleepingComputer further reported that three of the four initiators are also members of recently formed ransomware outfit Hellcat.

On Friday, 14 January 2025, a cyberattack was carried out by an unknown entity against the State Information Technology Centre (CTIE) in Luxembourg, affecting the availability of several government websites, including Guichet.lu, MyGuichet.lu, and government.lu, as well as the LuxTrust online banking service. The attack, identified as a DDoS attack, aimed at saturating servers with a large number of queries, occurred during a busy period of activity. It was detected by LuxTrust's protective measures shortly before 2 p.m. and countermeasures were activated. The situation was resolved between 4:30 pm. and 5:00 pm. The attack did not cause any security flaws. Dany Thielen, Communications Officer of the CTIE, and Stefano Susca, Chief Information Officer of LuxTrust, informed the public about the attack.

On Friday, 10 January 2025, the Swiss federal government was targeted by a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) cyber attack, which caused numerous federal websites to be unavailable for approximately 45 minutes. The attack, which was confirmed by the Federal IT Bureau (BIT), affected various websites, phone services, and Outlook, as well as other specialized applications. The BIT and the Federal Office for Cyber Security (BACS) took countermeasures to stabilize the situation and are currently further investigating the incident. According to the BIT, no data was compromised during the attack.

Eindhoven University of Technology was targeted by an unknown attacker, who breached the university's computer network on 11 January 2025 at 9 pm, prompting the university to shut down its network and suspend classes until at least 13 January 2025. The exact circumstances are not clear yet and subject to an ongoing internal investigation.

On 17 October 2024, the Polish IT security consulting company Securing sent a vulnerability note to Aviatrix that threat actors exploited a critical remote command execution vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2024-50603, in Aviatrix Controller instances, caused by inadequate use of input sanitization functions in some API actions, allowing attackers to inject malicious commands into system-level operations and install backdoors and crypto miners without authentication. The flaw affected all versions of Aviatrix Controller from 7.x through 7.2.4820. A proof-of-concept exploit was released on GitHub on 8 January 2025, which fuelled the exploitation of CVE-2024-50603, with hackers leveraging the flaw to plant Sliver backdoors and perform unauthorized Monero cryptocurrency mining using XMRig. On 7 November 2024, a patch was released and Aviatrix’ customers were notified. Wiz Research reported the exploitation on 13 January 2025, noting that most affected cloud enterprise environments constitute a risk for lateral network movement and privilege escalation.

Title (Company): Not available - Not available - Not available - Not available - Not available - Not available
Description: The state-sponsored threat actor RedDelta, also known as Mustang Panda/Bronze President/Stately Taurus/Earth Preta/TA416/HoneyMyte/Camaro Dragon, conducted targeted operations against government organizations and diplomatic entities in Taiwan, Mongolia, Southeast Asia, and Europe between July 2023 to December 2024, as stated in a Recorded Future Report from 9 January 2024. RedDelta used custom variants of PlugX malware and advanced attack methods, including DLL hijacking. Legitimate processes were exploited to load the malware without detection. Infection chains exploited MSI, DLL, and LNK files. The malware enabled data theft through system impairment and advanced persistence, allowing repeated access to the same devices. The operations likely compromised the Defense Ministry of Mongolia in August 2024 as well as Vietnam's communist party in November and targeted additional entities in Malaysia, Japan, the United States, Ethiopia, Brazil, Australia, and India without signs of compromise. The targeting is consistent with RedDelta's past behaviour aligning with goals of China's communist party.

On 14 January 2025, the Lynx group carried out a ransomware attack on Conad, an Italian consortium of independent retail enterprises. The attackers exfiltrated documents, including human resources and customer information, and threatened to make them public if Conad did not pay a ransom within 72 hours. The attack was claimed by the Lynx group on the Darkweb, with a countdown indicating the time available for Conad to contact the attackers and pay the ransom. The attack did not impact the operation of Conad's website and telematic services. The Lynx group published some documents as proof of the attack, including digitized versions of paper documents, specifications, and correspondence with customers and suppliers. Conad has not issued an official statement on the matter.

On 12 December 2024 and 17 December 2024, hackers breached the virtual hearing system of the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) in Mumbai by broadcasting pornographic content, disrupting proceedings. The incident came to light on 19 December 2024, when Mumbai's Cuffe Parade police registered a case after hackers gained unauthorized access to NCLT's online system. Charan Pratap Singh, the deputy registrar of NCLT Mumbai, filed a police complaint. The hackers used usernames 'Linda Z Miller' and 'Jonathan Adam Amelia' while broadcasting the obscene videos. The tribunal temporarily suspended virtual hearings, opting for physical hearings, causing delays and inconvenience to lawyers and litigants. Legal and cyber law experts reported the incident, expressing concerns about the vulnerability of Indian courts to cyberattacks and the need for stronger digital security measures.

Title (Company): PowerSchool - Edmonton Catholic School Division - Toronto District School Board - San Diego Unified School District - St. Albert Public Schools
Description: On December 28, 2024, Unknown Threat Actors breached the student information system vendor PowerSchool, affecting multiple school boards in the US and Canada. The attackers accessed names, birth dates, phone numbers, and home mailing addresses of students and families through PowerSchool's community-focused customer support portal, PowerSource. PowerSchool immediately engaged its cybersecurity response protocols and informed law enforcement. The company assured that no financial information was accessed, login information was not impacted, and the incident was contained. PowerSchool also stated that it had strengthened its security measures to prevent future breaches.

Title (Company): Ministero della Difesa - Amat of Palermo - Ministry of Infrastructure and Transport (Italy) - Siena Mobilita - Amt of Genoa - Port of Trieste - Ministry of Enterprises and Made in Italy (Italy) - Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena - Gruppo Torinese Trasporti (GTT) - Intesa Sanpaolo - Port of Taranto - Navy - Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation (Italy) - Italian Companies and Exchange Commission (Consob) - Carabinieri - Intesa Sanpaolo - ATAC Rome
Description: On 11 January 2025, the pro-Russian cyber criminal group NoName057(16) carried out a series of cyber attacks on Italian public institutions and companies. The attack targeted the websites of the ministries of Foreign Affairs, Infrastructure, and Transport, as well as the Carabinieri, Navy, and Air Force. Local public transport companies, including Atac of Rome, Amat of Palermo, and Amt of Genoa, were also affected. The group used DDoS attacks, causing temporary slowdowns in services. The following day, similar DDoS attacks were registered against various Italian companies, including the banks of Intesa Sanpaolo and Monte Paschi di Siena as well as ports of Taranto and Trieste. The attacks were announced by NoName057(16) on their Telegram channel and were linked to the visit of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to Italy, who arrived in Rome two days prior. Most of the attacks could be mitigated within hours the same day with support of the Italian Cybersecurity Agency ACN. From 14 to 17 July 2025, an international law enforcement operation code-named Eastwood was launched against NoName057(16). Coordinated by Europol and Eurojust, the operation involved simultaneous actions by authorities in Czechia, France, Finland, Germany, Italy, Lithuania, Poland, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, the Netherlands, and the United States, targeting individuals and digital infrastructure linked to the pro-Russian network. Operation Eastwood allowed for the deactivation of several hundred servers supporting the group’s DDoS activities. Overall, national authorities issued seven arrest warrants, including against six Russian nationals, over the suspected involvement in NoName057(16). The investigation further facilitated the arrest of two individuals in France and Spain. Law enforcement personally notified over 1,000 supporters of the group, including 15 suspected administrators, of their legal liability related to the participation in NoName057(16)‘s criminal activities.

Title (Company): Slovakian Geodesy, Cartography and Cadastre Office (UGKK)
Description: On January 7, 2025, the Slovakian Geodesy, Cartography and Cadastre Office (UGKK) was targeted by a ransomware attack, that shut down the agency's systems and closed its physical offices, with the attackers demanding millions of euros in ransom. The attack was reported by local media and confirmed by Agriculture Minister Richard Takac in a press conference on Friday, 10 January 2025, who assured that the systems would be restored with backups and that there is no risk of changes or fraudulent transcriptions of ownership data. Takac stated that this was the biggest cyberattack in the country's history and that there were "strong indications" that it originated from Ukraine, without providing any evidence or further details. Slovakia and Ukraine have been in a geopolitical dispute about Kyiv`s suspension of Russian gas transit through Slovakia at the time of the incident.

On Wednesday, January 8, 2025, Ivanti disclosed two vulnerabilities—CVE-2025-0282 and CVE-2025-0283—impacting Ivanti Connect Secure (ICS) VPN appliances. According to Mandiant, CVE-2025-0282 has been exploited in the wild as a zero-day vulnerability since mid-December 2024. This flaw is an unauthenticated stack-based buffer overflow, which, if successfully exploited, could allow unauthenticated remote code execution, potentially enabling further compromise of the affected network. During the analysis of at least one appliance, Mandiant identified the deployment of the SPAWN malware ecosystem, which includes the SPAWNANT installer, the SPAWNMOLE tunneler, and the SPAWNSNAIL SSH backdoor. The deployment of this malware ecosystem, following the targeting of Ivanti Secure Connect appliances, has been attributed to UNC5337—a cluster of activity assessed with moderate confidence to be part of UNC5221. Additionally, Mandiant discovered previously unknown malware families, now tracked as DRYHOOK and PHASEJAM, from other compromised appliances. These malware families have not yet been associated with any known group. Multiple actors may be involved in creating and deploying the SPAWN, DRYHOOK, and PHASEJAM code families. However, there is insufficient data to determine the number of threat actors targeting CVE-2025-0282, according to the Mandiant blog post.

Mortgage Investors Group (MIG), a Tennessee-based mortgage lender, was breached by the Black Basta Ransomware Gang in a cyberattack that started on 11 December 2024 and was discovered on 12 December 2024, resulting in the exposure of sensitive personal information, including full names and financial information, of an undisclosed number of customers. The company hired a vendor to identify affected individuals and notify them directly in several weeks.

Unknown Threat Actors carried out a cyberattack on the city of Winston-Salem, North Carolina, on December 26, 2024 knocking the city's systems offline, which was announced by city officials four days latter. The attack affected the city's digital payment systems for water and electricity bills, but did not disrupt fire and police response abilities. The city took down its digital platforms as a precaution and residents were advised to pay in person with cash or checks. The incident was reported by local news outlet WFDD, and city officials, including City Manager Pat Pate, who informed the city council about the attack. Federal agencies and the North Carolina National Guard were involved in the response effort. The attack occurred during a time of severe weather and freezing temperatures, causing issues with roadways and sanitation.

On January 9, 2025, the Ukrainian Cyber Alliance, a pro-Ukraine hacktivist group, breached Russian ISP Nodex, stealing sensitive documents and wiping systems, thereby destroying the company's connectivity. The attack was confirmed by Nodex, who speculated the involvement of Russia-linked threat actors, and by internet monitoring service NetBlocks, which reported a disruption in Nodex's connectivity. The Ukrainian Cyber Alliance published screenshots as proof of the breach, including images of the Veeam backup and Hewlett Packard Enterprise server consoles. Nodex informed the public about the attack through a message on VKontakte, stating that the network had been destroyed and was being restored from backup copies. The company later announced that it had restored its network core and was working to restore connections, but its website remained unreachable as of 9 January 2025. The attack affected fixed-line and mobile services.

Title (Company): Federal Service for State Registration, Cadastre and Cartography (Rosreestr)
Description: On January 9, 2025, a group of hackers known as Silent Crow claimed responsibility for breaching Rosreestr, a Russian government agency responsible for managing property and land records. The hackers released a portion of a database containing personal information of Russian citizens, including names, dates of birth, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, and individual insurance account numbers. Rosreestr denied the breach, but Russian investigative journalists from Agentstvo news outlet confirmed the legitimacy of the leaked data. The motivation behind the attack is unclear, but it is possible that Silent Crow is a pseudonym for a more well-known hacker group. The hackers warned of another attack and their Telegram channel was blocked shortly after the announcement. The incident was reported by Russian investigative journalists, including Andrey Soshnikov, editor-in-chief of Sistema, who noted that the scope of the leaked data could be extensive. The incident comes just week after an attack on similar databases in Ukraine attributed to Russian attackers.

In December 2024, an unknown threat actor targeted a Germany-based international manufacturer of electrical safety systems, known for its applications in hospitals, ships, wind turbines, and solar installations. The attackers stole sensitive data and demanded a ransom, threatening to publish the stolen information on 25 December 2024. The company, headquartered in Central Hesse with nearly 1,400 employees across multiple countries, has declined to comment. The Hessian Cybercrime Center (ZIT) and the local police's cybercrime unit are investigating the incident as a case of extortion. The company name has been withheld to protect affected employees and operations.

On 5 January 2025, the Kingston Police Service in Ontario, Canada, was affected by a cyber incident that impacted some of its IT systems, particularly non-emergency functions. The incident was first identified on Friday, 5 January 2025, and reported by Kingston police on 6 January 2025. The Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) Cybercrime Investigations Team is investigating the incident, with the assistance of third-party cybersecurity experts. Kingston police immediately implemented mitigation strategies to protect the public, staff, data, and organization. The Information and Privacy Commissioner was notified of the incident. The OPP and Kingston police stated that the ability to respond to emergency situations was not impacted.

On 23 December 2024, the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), suffered a significant data breach attributed to the cyber threat actor "Natohub." The attacker claimed responsibility and leaked data from a recruitment database containing over 42,000 records, affecting at least 11,929 individuals. Exposed information included names, contact details, dates of birth, addresses, and employment histories spanning from April 2016 to July 2024. Natohub released samples on a hacking forum, showcasing real names and titles. While ICAO confirmed the breach in January 2025, it emphasized that operational systems related to aviation safety and security were not impacted. The authenticity of all leaked data has not yet been fully verified. On 5 February 2025, the Spanish National Police arrested the individual hacker known as “Natohub” in the town of Calpe (Alicante).

At the beginning of December 2024, the controversial medical group Everyones Medical House was subjected to an extensive cyber attack by an unknown group of hackers, who exploited the access to steal person-sensitive information about patients. The attack resulted in patients being unable to log in or get in touch with their doctors' office. The clinic handled the attack with emergency preparedness to maintain acute functions and reported the case to the Data Protection Agency and the police on 30 December 2024. The incident was publicly disclosed by Everyones Doctors Office on their website on 30 December 2024, with experts, including IT security expert Jrn Guldberg and ethical hacker Michael Andersen, criticizing the three-week delay in informing the affected patients, citing increased risk of misuse of patients' data.

On 5 January 2025, the Upper Canada District School Board was targeted by a cyber attack, disrupting its network and preventing all schools under its jurisdiction from accessing the internet. The board contacted police and worked with trusted experts to assess the impact and restore services. The board informed the public about the attack on 6 January 2025. On 22 January, the UCDSB issued a statement confirming that personal information, including Date of birth, gender information, home address information and medical diagnosis and information about related needs for some students, had been exposed and began notifying those affected. On 20 February, UCDSB announced that the main services impacting students and families have been fully restored.

Chinese state-sponsored hackers breached U.S. Treasury Departmental Office's user workstations in December 2024, accessing unclassified documents in what Treasury officials described as a "major incident." According to a letter from 30 December in which the Treasury disclosed the incident to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs responsible for Congressional oversight, the hackers compromised BeyondTrust, a third-party cybersecurity provider, by gaining access to a key to secure a cloud-based service. This allowed them to override security measures, access user workstations remotely, and retrieve certain unclassified documents. In the letter, the Treasury attributed the breach to an APT group linked to China. Citing unidentified federal officials, The Washington Post reported Chinese hackers breached the Office of Foreign Assets Control, the Office of the Secretary of the Treasury and the Office of Financial Research in an apparent attempt to gather information on the U.S. government's future financial sanctions against Chinese companies. After detecting the breach in December, the Treasury previously told lawmakers it was forced to suspend cloud-based technical support services from a third-party contractor, BeyondTrust.  The Treasury Department learned of the breach on 8 December, when BeyondTrust alerted them. BeyondTrust detected potentially anomalous behaviour on 2 December 2024, confirmed after a root cause analysis on 5 December 2024. On 13 December, the company identified two zero-day vulnerabilities that allowed threat actors to gain privileged remote access and inject commands (CVE-2024-12356 and CVE-2024-12686). China's government denied involvement, with officials rejecting U.S. accusations and maintaining that Beijing opposes hacking. A Bloomberg Report from 8 January 2025 said the intrusion is linked to Silk Typhoon, citing anonymous sources within the US government. In a sanction communication issued on 17 Janaury 2025, the Treasury designated Yin Kecheng for his involvement in the compromise of its networks. The Treasury deems Yin to be affiliated with China's Ministry of State Security.

Unknown threat actors breached the IT systems of BayMark Health Services, the largest addiction treatment provider in the United States, between 24 September and 14 October 2024. The attackers stole personal and health information of an undisclosed number of patients, including names, Social Security numbers, driver's licence numbers, dates of birth, services received, insurance details, and treatment and diagnostic data. The breach was discovered on 11 October 2024 after an IT disruption and was later claimed by the RansomHub ransomware gang, which uploaded 1.5 TB of stolen files to its dark web leak site. BayMark began notifying affected patients on 8 January 2025 and offered one year of free identity monitoring services through Equifax.

On 2 January 2025, Japan's largest mobile carrier, NTT Docomo, was targeted by a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack. The attack temporarily disrupted some of its services, including its news website, video streaming platform, mobile payment, webmail services, and a golf enthusiasts website. These services were unavailable from early Thursday morning until late afternoon. NTT Docomo reported the incident and worked to restore full operations, with access to most services restored, although some content updates might still face delays.

On December 29, 2023, Medusind, a U.S. medical billing provider, discovered suspicious activity within its IT network and immediately took the affected systems offline. With the help of a cybersecurity forensic firm, the company investigated the breach and found evidence that unknown threat actors may have obtained a copy of certain files containing personal information of over 360,000 individuals, including health insurance and billing information, payment information, health information, government identification, and other personal information. The breach was publically disclosed by Medusind on January 7, 2025, and the company implemented enhanced security measures to prevent similar incidents. The attack was reported by Medusind, but it is unclear if the company was the victim of a ransomware attack, and no ransomware gang claimed responsibility for the attack.

Title (Company): South Portland Public Schools - Rutherford County Schools (RCS)
Description: Rutherford County Schools (RCS) in Tennessee experienced a network and systems disruption on 25 November 2024.  In the first media reports in early December 2024, the school centre was still investigating the source of the disruption in collaboration with the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation (TBI).  On 27 December 2024, the school district reported that a third-party IT security company had determined that unauthorised acquisition of some employee and student information had occurred.

On December 24, 2024, the pro-Iranian hacktivist group Handala breached ReutOne, a small Microsoft 365 Dynamics reseller, reported Kevin Beaumont on December 27, 2024. Accordingly, they exploited the breach by sending fraudulent emails to ReutOne's customers in Israel, France, and Ukraine, urging them to install fake software updates. The fake update was malware. Once installed, it connected to external servers and gathered system information if specific criteria were met. It executed various commands, such as retrieving system details, querying user and network information, accessing stored credentials, and inspecting firewall states. The collected data was then sent to a command-and-control (C2) server. The attackers engaged in "hands-on keyboard" activities, potentially manually interacting with unspecified compromised systems.  At the time of Beaumont's blog post on December 27, 2024, major antimalware vendors were still unable to detect the payload effectively, demonstrating poor static detection capabilities. However, additional investigation uncovered further victim organizations and indicators of compromise (IoCs). On January 2, 2024, the hacker group Handala claimed on Twitter to have accessed the database of hundreds of so called ‘Zionist’ companies.

Title (Company): Department of Haute-Garonne - Commune of Tarbes - City of Marseille
Description: On December 31, 2024, coordinated cyberattacks disrupted municipal websites in several major French cities. A pro-Russian hacking group known as NoName claimed responsibility, framing the attacks as a protest against France's support for Ukraine. The attacks initially brought down websites for Marseille, Tarbes, and the Haute-Garonne department. NoName later claimed on X  to have targeted 23 sites, including those of Nantes, Bordeaux, Nice, Montpellier, French Polynesia, and New Caledonia. While many websites were restored by the end of the day, the disruptions prompted an investigation by the Paris prosecutor's office. From 14 to 17 July 2025, an international law enforcement operation code-named Eastwood was launched against NoName057(16). Coordinated by Europol and Eurojust, the operation involved simultaneous actions by authorities in Czechia, France, Finland, Germany, Italy, Lithuania, Poland, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, the Netherlands, and the United States, targeting individuals and digital infrastructure linked to the pro-Russian network. Operation Eastwood allowed for the deactivation of several hundred servers supporting the group’s DDoS activities. Overall, national authorities issued seven arrest warrants, including against six Russian nationals, over the suspected involvement in NoName057(16). The investigation further facilitated the arrest of two individuals in France and Spain. Law enforcement personally notified over 1,000 supporters of the group, including 15 suspected administrators, of their legal liability related to the participation in NoName057(16)‘s criminal activities.

Title (Company): Manisa News Agency - Manisa Pocket TV
Description: On January 5, 2025, Manisa News Agency and Manisa Pocket TV were attacked by the 'Illegal Platform' group. The attackers used a photo of Soma Mayor Sercan Okur and posted anticapitalism statements. Mayor Okur denied any involvement, stating his name and photo were used without his consent, and announced he would follow the legal process. Manisa News Agency officials filed a criminal complaint. The 'Illegal Platform' group claimed the incident, stating they were not affiliated with other organizations like Anonymous.

On 26 December 2024, Japan Airlines (JAL) suffered a cyber attack on its communications networks, causing a failure in its systems that resulted in delays in both domestic and international flights. The attack, which was detected at 07:24 local time, affected at least 14 domestic flights, with delays of up to one hour, and also impacted international flights. The airline's baggage check-in system was disrupted, and ticket sales were temporarily suspended. JAL identified and addressed the cause of the issue, and resumed ticket sales for domestic and international flights. The airline's security of operations was not affected, and the company temporarily shut down the compromised router. The incident was disclosed by JAL in a statement, and the Chief Cabinet Secretary Yoshimasa Hayashi asked JAL to repair its system as soon as possible to respond adequately to the affected customers. The origin of the cyberattack is still under investigation.

On 23-26 September 2024, American Addiction Centers was breached by a ransomware attack claimed by the Rhysida ransomware group, resulting in the exposure of sensitive healthcare information of 422,424 people. The attack was discovered on 26 September 2024. The stolen data included Social Security numbers, health insurance information, names, addresses, phone numbers, and medical record numbers. The company mailed out breach notification letters to the affected individuals ahead of the Christmas holiday. Breach notices were filed in Texas, where over 26,000 people were impacted, and California.

On 19 December 2024, a cyber attack attributed to Russian state-sponsored actors linked to the GRU temporarily disrupted Ukraine's state registries, managed by the Ministry of Justice. The attack, described as the largest of its kind on the country's registries, suspended online services for administrative matters like marriages, car registrations, and changes of residence. Deputy Prime Minister and Justice Minister Olha Stefanishyna stated the attack aimed to "instill panic among Ukrainian citizens and those abroad" and noted it had been prepared for several months. While no data leaks or thefts have been confirmed, all registries remain offline as a precautionary measure. Restoration efforts are underway, with basic services expected to resume within two weeks. Ukrainian authorities, including the SSU, are conducting a criminal investigation, with suspicions centered on a GRU-affiliated hacker group.

The Chinese National Internet Emergency Response Center (CNCERT) reported two cyberattacks on December 18, 2024, in which the United States stole trade secrets. In the second incident, suspected U.S. intelligence agencies have targeted a major high-tech enterprise in China's smart energy and digital information sector since May 2023. The attackers exploited vulnerabilities in Microsoft Exchange to hack into and control the company's mail servers, implanting backdoors to steal email data continuously. They also used the compromised mail servers as a springboard to attack and control over 30 devices belonging to the company and its subsidiaries. As a result, the attackers stole a significant amount of the company’s trade secret information. The incident involved using multiple overseas platforms to mask the attack's origin.

The Chinese National Internet Emergency Response Center (CNCERT) reported two cyberattacks on December 18, 2024, involving the theft of trade secrets by the United States. In the first cyber incident, a Chinese advanced materials design and research unit has allegedly been targeted by U.S. intelligence agencies since August 2024. The attackers exploited a vulnerability in an electronic document security management system, compromising the company's software upgrade management server. Through this breach, they delivered control Trojans to over 270 company hosts via the software upgrade service, stealing significant amounts of trade secret information and intellectual property.

Title (Company): Attorney General's Office of Nuevo León
Description: In March 2024, a hacker breached the computer system of the Attorney General's Office of Nuevo León, accessing 960 folders and stealing approximately 14.7 GB worth of information containing sensitive data, including photos of corpses and identifications. The attack was detected in March 2024, and an internal investigation was initiated. The Nuevo León Attorney General's Office kept the cyber incident hidden for nine months until the breach was revealed through social media.  The incident was publicly disclosed on 17 December 2024 by the Attorney General's Office of Nuevo León. They claim to have gathered key evidence, including videos and documents, leading to the identification of possible perpetrators and the issuing of arrest warrants.

Title (Company): Not available - Not available - Not available
Description: Unit 42 researchers uncovered a phishing campaign targeting European companies, particularly in Germany and the UK, within the automotive, chemical, and industrial compound manufacturing sectors from June 2024 to at least September 2024. Palo Alto Networks reported the campaign and its findings on 18 December 2024. The campaign aimed to harvest account credentials to take over victims' Microsoft Azure cloud infrastructure. Attackers used phishing emails containing malicious PDFs or HTML links created via the HubSpot Free Form Builder service. Victims who clicked these links were redirected to credential-harvesting pages disguised as legitimate Microsoft login portals. The campaign targeted approximately 20,000 users. Once credentials were stolen, attackers used them to access Microsoft Azure accounts, perform lateral movements, and establish persistent control, even during active efforts to block access. The attackers also used VPN proxies to mask their origins and mimic logins from trusted locations.
Techniques Used: Content Injection, Drive-by Compromise, Phishing, Valid Accounts

Description: On the night of 11 December 2024, a cyberattack was directed towards the April supermarket chain, resulting in moderate impacts on the operations of the Granby-based banner. The attack caused long queues in the stores during the weekend of 14-15 December 2024, with a limited number of cases in service, and employees had to enter product codes manually. The company, with 13 addresses in Quebec, was conducting an in-depth analysis with cybersecurity experts to determine what has been affected in their systems. The attack has slowed down some activities, with some cases closed in all branches, but supermarkets remain open and operational. The incident was disclosed by Serge Gauthier, Executive Vice-President, in an email sent to Le Soleil on 17 December 2024. At the time of reporting on December 17, 2024, there is no indication that personal information from employees and clients was disclosed during the cyberattack.

On December 8, 2024, French digital services company Ecritel faced a cyberattack claimed by ransomware group Hunters International on December 17, 2024. The group alleged the theft of 270 GB of sensitive data, including contractual documents, network architecture diagrams, IT administration tool interfaces, and Ecritel’s information system security plan (ISSP). Despite these claims, Ecritel reported that the attack was swiftly detected and thwarted without disrupting business continuity or customer platforms. Ecritel's investigation, supported by a PASSI-certified third-party audit, concluded that only an internal server containing employee working documents was compromised and partially exfiltrated.

On 17 December 2024, the Russian DDoS gang NoName057(16) launched a DDoS campaign against several German companies, including weapons manufacturer Walther, energy company Vattenfall Group, a wood-based materials manufacturer, automotive suppliers, and a construction chemicals company. The attackers temporarily disrupted their websites' accessibility, using the attacks as a political message rather than extorting ransom money. The day before, the flood of parcels had targeted two German federal authorities, among others: The Federal Commissioner for Data Protection and Freedom of Information (BfDI) and the Federal Network Agency were allegedly attacked by a Russian support group.

ConnectOnCall, a telehealth platform, was breached between 16 February 2024 and 12 May 2024, exposing personal and medical information of over 900,000 individuals. The breach, discovered on 12 May 2024, included names, phone numbers, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, medical record numbers, and health-related information. ConnectOnCall hired cybersecurity experts, notified federal law enforcement, and took its product offline to restore it in a secure environment. The company notified impacted individuals and offered them identity and credit monitoring services through Kroll, with notice letters mailed on 11 December 2024.

Unknown threat actors launched a cyberattack on Ingolstädter Klinikum, a hospital in Bavaria, in December 2024. The hospital's IT department detected and contained the intrusion in its early phase, successfully preventing the spread of the attack. According to a statement issued on 17 December, no patient data was stolen or encrypted, and no ransom demands were made. The incident was first made public through a press release on 10 December 2024.

On 13 December 2024, hackers from China hacked the Facebook account of the municipality of Arauco, forcing officials to file a complaint with the Investigations Police of Chile (PDI). The attackers changed the fan page's name to 'Pet World', uploaded pet content in English, and stole data. The PDI informed the municipality of a massive attack from China targeting the social media platforms of public entities with many followers. The hackers' goal was likely to sell the accounts online. The municipality recovered some posts and created a backup account, 'Municipality of Arauco 2.0', to continue sharing content with their neighbours.

South Asian threat actor TA397 (also known as Bitter) gained access to a Turkish defence sector organisation using WmRAT and MiyaRAT beginning on November 18, 2024, U.S. IT-security company Proofpoint reported on December 17, 2024. The attack began with a spear-phishing email containing a RAR archive disguised as a public infrastructure initiative by the World Bank in Madagascar. TA397 manually deployed two remote access trojans (RATs), WmRAT and MiyaRAT, to enable intelligence gathering and data exfiltration. Proofpoint attributed this campaign to intelligence collection efforts likely supporting a South Asian government.

Between 5 September 2024 and 4 November 2024, unknown threat actors, later identified as the Nitrogen ransomware gang, compromised SRP Federal Credit Union's systems, potentially accessing files containing sensitive personal and financial data, including names, Social Security numbers, driver’s licence numbers, dates of birth, and account information. The breach affected approximately 240,000 individuals. SRP detected the incident and notified law enforcement, initiating an investigation that concluded on 22 November 2024. On 5 December 2024, Nitrogen claimed responsibility for the attack and alleged they had exfiltrated 650 GB of customer data.

Amnesty International conducted a forensic analysis of the Android phone belonging to Serbian journalist Slaviša Milanov, who suspected tampering by Serbian authorities. Milanov, an investigative journalist from Dimitrovgrad working with the FAR news portal, focuses on sensitive topics such as local government spending and corruption. On February 21, 2024, Milanov and a colleague were stopped by traffic police en route to a business meeting in Pirot. He was taken to the police station for additional tests for alcohol and drugs, which were conducted after a 20-minute delay and returned negative results. During his time at the station, Milanov was asked to leave his belongings, including his phone, and was later questioned by two men in civilian clothes about his journalistic work and the financing of FAR. Following the questioning, his devices were returned, but Milanov noticed unusual behavior on his phone, such as mobile data and Wi-Fi being turned off and excessive battery use by certain apps. Suspecting unauthorized access, Milanov installed a security app, which revealed that some apps were accessed and new ones installed while he was in custody. Amnesty International’s Security Lab confirmed that NoviSpy spyware apps were covertly installed on his Xiaomi Redmi Note 10S during his detention. The analysis also found evidence that Cellebrite’s UFED forensic tool was used to unlock the phone, enabling the spyware installation.

In November 2024, Amnesty International conducted a forensic analysis of the phone belonging to Nikola Ristić, a youth activist. The analysis confirmed that the phone was infected with NoviSpy spyware after being unlocked using Cellebrite UFED while in Serbian authorities' custody. Nikola was a key organizer of a protest in Belgrade following the tragic collapse of a train station roof in Novi Sad, which killed 14 people and injured dozens on November 1, 2024. On November 3, Nikola and his partner arrived at Belgrade’s Trg Republike carrying red paint for the protest. Shortly after, they were stopped by four men who identified themselves as BIA officers. Despite Nikola’s initial resistance due to the absence of a warrant, he was taken to a police station after a brief altercation, during which an officer threatened him and acted aggressively. Nikola’s belongings, including his phone, were confiscated at the station. During questioning, officers returned his phone and instructed him to call his partner to request the removal of a video of his arrest circulating on social media. After the call, his phone was taken out of the room. Nikola was interrogated; he perceived the questioning as a tactic to waste time, and no court order was presented to justify his detention. He was released after over two hours, around 1:30 PM. Suspicious of tampering, Nikola contacted Amnesty International’s Security Lab. Forensic analysis of his Huawei Honor 20 Pro revealed traces of NoviSpy spyware installed during his detention, with evidence showing physical access to his device via the Android ADB protocol.  One week after the infection, the spyware was still active, and logs indicated that operators had reconfigured it to upload data every three minutes, showing active device management. The analysis also confirmed that Cellebrite UFED was used to unlock the phone before the spyware installation. Amnesty International reported on many cyber incidents against Serbian civil society. Amnesty International attributed this cyber incident to the Serbian Security Intelligence Agency (BIA). Amnesty International also wrote that Google was able to identify further incidents, i.e. incidents outside of the ones mentioned in the Amnesty International report. Amnesty International also assumes additional compromises based on the sample numbers of the malware.

Amnesty International investigated a case involving an activist from the NGO Krokodil who suspected tampering with their phone following an October 2024 interview with Serbian BIA officials. Krokodil, an organization advocating for reconciliation in the Western Balkans and openly supporting Ukrainian and Russian dissidents, has faced frequent threats and vandalism, including a September 2024 incident where Russian-speaking intruders removed a Ukrainian flag from their office. On October 1, 2024, after requesting a meeting with BIA regarding the incident, the activist was interviewed at the Ministry of Interior in Belgrade. Before the questioning, BIA officials asked the activist to restart their phone, which he unlocked using a pattern-based PIN. Although the officials could not visibly observe the unlock pattern, room cameras likely captured it. During the interview, which lasted from 10:17 to 11:40, the activist’s phone was left unattended in their jacket outside the room. Upon leaving the interview, the activist noticed suspicious activity on their Samsung Galaxy S24+, including a notification that their contacts had been exported at 10:38. Confronting BIA officials yielded denials, prompting the activist to seek Amnesty International’s Security Lab assistance. Forensic analysis confirmed that two spyware applications, NoviSpyAdmin and NoviSpyAccess, were installed on the phone during the interview. Logs revealed that at 10:20, the phone was powered on shortly after the interview began and connected to a ThinkPad X1 Yoga via USB. Authorities used the Android ADB protocol to gain control, disable security features, and manually browse the device, including its photo gallery, while exporting contacts. NoviSpyAdmin, a device admin app, collected sensitive data such as call logs, contacts, SMS messages, and audio recordings. NoviSpyAccess exploited Android accessibility features to capture screenshots, track location, exfiltrate files, and activate the phone’s camera. By 10:27, NoviSpyAccess was configured as the active accessibility service, enabling comprehensive surveillance. The spyware remained active on the device at the time of Amnesty International’s analysis, uploading screenshots of sensitive information, including emails, Signal and WhatsApp messages, and social media activity, to a spyware server. Data logs confirmed that NoviSpy communicated with IP addresses linked to Telekom Srbija, a government-controlled ISP. Amnesty International reported on many cyber incidents against Serbian civil society. Amnesty International attributed this cyber incident to the Serbian Security Intelligence Agency  (BIA). Amnesty International also wrote that Google was able to identify further incidents, i.e. incidents outside of the ones mentioned in the Amnesty International report. Amnesty International also assumes additional compromises based on the sample numbers of the malware.

Beginning since at least April 29, 2024, Chinese threat actor Winnti Group was found to be using a PHP-based backdoor called 'Glutton' to target the cybercriminal underground, primarily in China. The backdoor, which shares similarities with the Winnti backdoor, was discovered by researchers at QiAnXin XLab, who reported the incident on December 12, 2024. Glutton was found to be embedded in an archive downloaded from the Timibbs cybercrime online market and linked to a fraudulent click-farming platform. The backdoor can extract sensitive system data, deploy an Executable and Linkable Format backdoor, and inject malicious code into PHP frameworks like Baota, ThinkPHP, Yii and Laravel. The attackers used poisoned tools to turn cybercrime operators into unwitting pawns, with the malware operating stealthily within PHP or PHP-FPM FastCGI processes. The victims of Glutton span various sectors, particularly in IT services and business operations, and include systems used by cyber criminals, with the majority of them located in China.

Title (Company): Texas Tech University Health Sciences Center El Paso - Texas Tech University Health Sciences Center
Description: In September 2024, the Interlock ransomware group breached the Texas Tech University Health Sciences Center and its El Paso counterpart, disrupting computer systems and applications and exfiltrating sensitive data between 17 and 29 September. The attack potentially exposed the personal and medical data of approximately 1.4 million patients, including full names, dates of birth, physical addresses, Social Security numbers, driver’s licence and government ID numbers, financial and health insurance information, as well as billing, diagnosis, and treatment records. The incident was reported to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office for Civil Rights and publicly disclosed on 16 December 2024. On 27 October 2024, the attackers leaked 2.1 million files totalling 2.6 TB of data on the dark web.

Hunters International ransomware gang breached the confidentiality of Telecom Namibia, Namibia's state-owned telecom provider, by conducting a ransomware attack at the end of November 2024. It resulted in the leak of over 400,000 files, including personal and financial data of high-ranking government officials and clients, after Telecom Namibia refused to negotiate a ransom, with the data being made public on the dark web. Some of it was circulating on social media, as reported by local media and confirmed by Telecom Namibia's chief executive, Stanley Shanapinda, on December 16, 2024. Hunters International claimed the ransomware attack on December 10, 2024.

On 14 December 2024, Turkey's highway and bridge transit system, HGS, suffered a major cyber attack by the hacker group 'hades_hgs'. The attackers infiltrated the HGS database, stealing personal and financial data of over 5 million users, which was subsequently shared on the Dark Web. The group demanded a ransom of $25,000 and threatened to release additional sensitive information, including over a million credit card records, if their demands were not met. The attack is reportedly linked to a dispute involving a lawyer named 'Juadis.' On December 16, 2024, various Turkish media reported on the detainment of two suspects linked to the beach of the Turkish Highway and Bridge Transit System (HGS). Involved law enforcement authorities, namely the Denizli and Mersin Provincial Gendarmerie Commands coordinated by the Department of Combating Cybercrimes and in cooperation with the National Intelligence Organization (MIT) and the Information and Communication Technologies Authority (BTK) and the Computer Emergency Response Team of Turkey (TR-CERT), detained Veli B. (also known as Hades) and Burak K. (also known as Klew) on suspicion of unauthorized access to information systems and sharing messages insulting national and religious values. During the investigation, Veli B. was arrested, while Burak K. was released under judicial control. It was noted that Burak K. admitted on social media that the cyber attack was carried out as a joke.

On 27 November 2024, Argentina's National Atomic Energy Commission (CNEA) was targeted in a ransomware attack attributed to the Money Message strain, first identified in 2023. The attack impacted all CNEA headquarters, encrypting data and disrupting the organization’s administrative network. The attackers demanded a cryptocurrency ransom in exchange for a decryptor. Although the CNEA assured that no project-related information was accessed, experts warn that data breaches often lead to leaks on the dark web shortly after such incidents. The Argentine government acknowledged the attack, and an official investigation is underway by the judiciary, with additional oversight from the Access to Public Information Agency

On 13 November 2024, unknown threat actors breached the information technology systems of LKQ Corporation’s Canadian business unit, causing data theft and operational disruptions that lasted for several weeks. LKQ, a major U.S.-based provider of auto parts with over 1,600 locations and 45,000 employees worldwide, immediately launched an investigation, partnered with forensic experts, and notified law enforcement authorities. While the affected business unit has since returned to near full capacity, LKQ disclosed the incident in a Form 8-K filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on 14 December 2024. The company stated that the incident is not expected to have a material impact on its financial condition for the fiscal year and confirmed its plans to seek reimbursement through its cybersecurity insurance.

On 5 December 2024, unknown perpetrators targeted Rhode Island's public benefits system, RIBridges, managed by Deloitte, in a ransomware attack that compromised personal and financial data. The breach, confirmed on 10 December, exposed sensitive information, including names, addresses, birth dates, Social Security numbers, and bank details of individuals who applied for or received benefits such as Medicaid, SNAP, and TANF. The state proactively shut down RIBridges on 13 December after discovering malicious code, halting the system's operations to contain the threat. Although no identity theft has been reported, Governor Dan McKee urged vigilance and offered free credit monitoring to affected households. A dedicated call center and website updates have been established to assist impacted residents

A likely China-based threat actor gained access to multiple organisations in Southeast Asia beginning at least as early as October 2023, Symantec reported on 11 December 2024. The affected organisations were government ministries in two unnamed countries, an air traffic control organisation, a telecommunications company and a media outlet.  The threat actor exfiltrated likely data of interest. Symantec became aware of this cyber incident on 27 May 2024 when a suspicious PowerShell command was executed.

In December 2024, unknown threat actors, later identified as the RA World Ransomware gang, launched a ransomware attack against Compass Communications, a New Zealand-based telecommunications provider. The attack compromised both the confidentiality and integrity of the company's systems, with the attackers claiming to have exfiltrated 250 gigabytes of internal and customer data, including financial records, customer details, human resources files, and information on ongoing projects. As evidence of the breach, a 26.9-megabyte archive of sample data was posted on the gang's darknet leak site. Compass Communications confirmed the breach to Cyber Daily, revealing that their security monitoring had detected unauthorised access to their systems the previous week. The company promptly engaged external cybersecurity experts and notified relevant government authorities. An initial investigation suggested that some customer information may have been accessed. The RA World Ransomware gang set a ransom deadline of 1 January 2025.

In late 2023 and mid-2024, Iranian threat actors, specifically the CyberAv3ngers group, used a new malware named IOCONTROL to compromise Internet of Things (IoT) devices and OT/SCADA systems in Israel and the United States, Claroty's Team82 reported on December 10, 2024. The targeted devices included routers, programmable logic controllers (PLCs), human-machine interfaces (HMIs), IP cameras, firewalls, and fuel management systems from various manufacturers, including D-Link, Hikvision, Baicells, Red Lion, Orpak, Phoenix Contact, Teltonika, and Unitronics.  On 14 October 2024, the threat actors claimed to have compromised 200 gas stations in Israel and the U.S. on Telegram, which aligns with Claroty's findings. Claroty's Team82 confirmed that the threat actors compromised several hundred Israeli-made Orpak systems and U.S.-made Gasyboy fuel management systems. This happened in one go from mid-October 2023 to January 2024 until they resumed their attack from July to August 2024.

On November 18, 2024, US Bitcoin ATM operator Byte Federal became aware that unknown threat actors gained access to one of their servers, exploiting a GitLab vulnerability, potentially compromising the personal information of 58,000 customers, including name, birthdate, address, phone number, email address, government-issued ID, social security number, transaction activity, and photographs of users.  Byte Federal disclosed the data breach and responded by shutting down its platform, locking out the attacker, and securing the compromised server.

On 29 November 2024, unknown threat actors compromised the confidentiality and availability of Krispy Kreme's information technology systems, disrupting online ordering across the United States. Krispy Kreme, which operates 1,521 shops and 15,800 points of access, detected unauthorized activity and engaged leading cybersecurity experts to address the incident.
